#10886. AI reads brain MRIs in seconds and flags emergencies

A newly developed artificial intelligence system from the University of Michigan can analyze brain MRI scans and deliver a diagnosis in a matter of seconds, according to a new study. The model identified neurological conditions with accuracy reaching 97.5% and was also able to assess how urgently patients needed medical care.

Researchers say this first-of-its-kind technology has the potential to reshape how brain imaging is handled across health systems in the United States. The findings were published in Nature Biomedical Engineering.

"As the global demand for MRI rises and places significant strain our physicians and health systems, our AI model has potential to reduce burden by improving diagnosis and treatment with fast, accurate information," said senior author Todd Hollon, M.D., a neurosurgeon at University of Michigan Health and assistant professor of neurosurgery at U-M Medical School.

Hollon named the new technology Prima. Over a one-year period, his research team evaluated the system using more than 30,000 MRI studies.

Across more than 50 different radiologic diagnoses involving major neurological disorders, Prima delivered stronger diagnostic performance than other advanced AI models. In addition to identifying disease, the system also proved capable of determining which cases required higher priority.

Certain neurological conditions, including strokes and brain hemorrhages, demand immediate medical attention. Hollon said that in these situations, Prima can automatically alert health care providers so action can be taken quickly.

The system was designed to notify the most appropriate subspecialist, such as a stroke neurologist or neurosurgeon. Feedback becomes available immediately after a patient completes imaging.

"Accuracy is paramount when reading a brain MRI, but quick turnaround times are critical for timely diagnosis and improved outcomes," said Yiwei Lyu, M.S., co-first author and postdoctoral fellow of Computer Science and Engineering at U-M.

"At key steps in the process, our results show how Prima can improve workflows and streamline clinical care without abandoning accuracy."

Prima is classified as a vision language model (VLM), a type of artificial intelligence that can process images, video, and text together in real time. While artificial intelligence has been applied to MRI analysis before, researchers say Prima takes a different approach.

Earlier models were typically trained on carefully selected subsets of MRI data and designed to perform narrow tasks, such as identifying lesions or estimating dementia risk. Prima was trained on a much broader dataset.

Hollon's team used every available MRI collected since radiology records were digitized at University of Michigan Health. This included more than 200,000 MRI studies and 5.6 million imaging sequences. The model also incorporated patients' clinical histories and the reasons physicians ordered each imaging study.

"Prima works like a radiologist by integrating information regarding the patient's medical history and imaging data to produce a comprehensive understanding of their health," said co-first author Samir Harake, a data scientist in Hollon's Machine Learning in Neurosurgery Lab.

"This enables better performance across a broad range of prediction tasks."

Addressing MRI Delays and Radiology Shortages

Each year, millions of MRI scans are performed worldwide, many of them focused on neurological disease. Researchers say the demand for these scans is growing faster than the availability of neuroradiology services.

This imbalance has contributed to staffing shortages, diagnostic delays, and errors. Depending on where a patient receives a scan, results may take days or even longer to return.

"Whether you are receiving a scan at a larger health system that is facing increasing volume or a rural hospital with limited resources, innovative technologies are needed to improve access to radiology services," said Vikas Gulani, M.D. Ph.D., co-author and chair of the Department of Radiology at U-M Health.

"Our teams at University of Michigan have collaborated to develop a cutting-edge solution to this problem with tremendous, scalable potential."

Although Prima performed strongly, researchers emphasize that the work is still in an early evaluation phase. Future research will focus on incorporating more detailed patient information and electronic medical record data to further improve diagnostic accuracy.

This approach mirrors how radiologists and physicians interpret MRIs and other imaging studies in real clinical settings. While artificial intelligence is already used in health care, most existing systems are limited to narrowly defined tasks.

Hollon describes Prima as "ChatGPT for medical imaging," noting that similar technology could eventually be adapted for other imaging types, including mammograms, chest X-rays and ultrasounds.

"Like the way AI tools can help draft an email or provide recommendations, Prima aims to be a co-pilot for interpreting medical imaging studies," Hollon said.

"We believe that Prima exemplifies the transformative potential of integrating health systems and AI-driven models to improve health care through innovation."

Additional authors: Asadur Chowdury, M.S., Soumyanil Banerjee, M.S., Rachel Gologorsky, Shixuan Liu, Anna-Katharina Meissner, M.D., Akshay Rao, Chenhui Zhao, Akhil Kondepudi, Cheng Jiang, Xinhai Hou, Rushikesh S. Joshi, M.D., Volker Neuschmelting, M.D., Ashok Srinivasan, M.D., Dawn Kleindorfer, M.D., Brian Athey, Ph.D., Aditya Pandey, M.D., and Honglak Lee, Ph.D., all of University of Michigan.

Funding/disclosures: This work was supported in part by the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (K12NS080223) of the National Institutes of Health.

#10884. Indie game platform itch.io says it deleted “a couple terabytes” of AI slop

Indie game platform itch.io has revealed that it deleted several terabytes of AI-generated content from its website as concerns grow over the increasing number of games being created using artificial intelligence.

The platform, which allows independent developers to upload and distribute their games, has guidelines restricting excessive amounts of automatically generated content, including projects created with minimal human involvement.

The announcement comes as other gaming storefronts face similar concerns. A recent analysis found that nearly half of all new games released on Steam in October 2026 disclosed using AI-generated content.

“Just deleted a couple terabytes of ai slop,” itch.io wrote in a November 2 post on X, which attracted more than 1.6 million views.

The platform did not specify how many games or projects were affected or provide details about the individual uploads that were deleted.

Just deleted a couple terabytes of ai slop 😌

Under its existing quality guidelines, itch.io warns developers against using automated systems to mass-produce product pages, which it considers spam.

This includes games predominantly created by AI with minimal human involvement, randomly generated content with little curated design, and multiple versions of essentially identical AI-generated projects.

Developers are also required to disclose their use of generative AI through a dedicated section on their project’s editing page. Those that do so are listed under an “AI Assisted” browsing category.

However, the platform does not prohibit all uses of AI. Its guidelines state that developers can use automatically generated content as long as it adds substantial value to the experience and is clearly disclosed.

Just because you can upload 10 terabytes of poorly optimized ai generated models doesn't mean you should upload 10 terabytes of poorly optimized ai generated modelsAs a reminder we have had an AI spam clause in our quality guidelines for over two years: https://t.co/THyyRJarKu

Traditional game systems, including NPC pathfinding, enemy behavior, and procedural level generation, are not classified as generative AI under these rules.

Publisher blames “AI-slop” on Steam as their game only gets 15 players at launch

Almost half of all new Steam games use AI now

Indie dev says Google AI somehow leaked detail about their game that was totally private

The cleanup comes amid growing concerns about AI-generated games on Steam, where an analysis of approximately 63,600 releases found that 49.9% of games launched in October 2026 disclosed using AI, compared to just 1.7% in January 2024.

Some developers have also raised concerns about how the increasing number of submissions could affect smaller studios.

On November 2, indie publisher 2 Left Thumbs blamed a “tidal wave of AI-slop” for allegedly overwhelming Steam’s review process and delaying the release of its co-op game Wheel Make It.

Despite accumulating more than 11,000 wishlists before launch, the game peaked at just 15 concurrent players in the 24 hours after its November 1 release.

The publisher argued that the delay damaged the game’s launch visibility, although Valve has not confirmed that AI-generated submissions were responsible for the review backlog.

#10882. Brain inspired machines are better at math than expected

Computers designed to mimic the structure of the human brain are showing an unexpected strength. They can solve some of the demanding mathematical equations that lie at the heart of major scientific and engineering problems.

In a study published in Nature Machine Intelligence, Sandia National Laboratories computational neuroscientists Brad Theilman and Brad Aimone introduced a new algorithm that allows neuromorphic hardware to solve partial differential equations, or PDEs -- the mathematical foundation for modeling phenomena such as fluid dynamics, electromagnetic fields and structural mechanics.

The results demonstrate that neuromorphic systems can handle these equations efficiently. The advance could help open the door to the first neuromorphic supercomputer, offering a new path toward energy efficient computing for national security and other critical applications.

The research was funded by the Department of Energy's Office of Science through the Advanced Scientific Computing Research and Basic Energy Sciences programs, as well as the National Nuclear Security Administration's Advanced Simulation and Computing program.

Solving Partial Differential Equations With Brain Like Hardware

Partial differential equations are essential for simulating real world systems. They are used to forecast weather, analyze how materials respond to stress, and model complex physical processes. Traditionally, solving PDEs requires enormous computing power. Neuromorphic computers approach the problem differently by processing information in ways that resemble how the brain operates.

"We're just starting to have computational systems that can exhibit intelligent-like behavior. But they look nothing like the brain, and the amount of resources that they require is ridiculous, frankly," Theilman said.

For years, neuromorphic systems were mainly viewed as tools for pattern recognition or for speeding up artificial neural networks. Few expected them to manage mathematically rigorous problems such as PDEs, which are typically handled by large scale supercomputers.

Aimone and Theilman were not surprised by the outcome. They argue that the human brain routinely carries out highly complex calculations, even if people are unaware of it.

"Pick any sort of motor control task -- like hitting a tennis ball or swinging a bat at a baseball," Aimone said. "These are very sophisticated computations. They are exascale-level problems that our brains are capable of doing very cheaply."

Energy Efficient Computing for National Security

The findings could have major implications for the National Nuclear Security Administration, which is responsible for maintaining the nation's nuclear deterrent. Supercomputers used across the nuclear weapons complex consume vast amounts of electricity to simulate the physics of nuclear systems and other high stakes scenarios.

Neuromorphic computing may provide a way to significantly cut energy use while still delivering strong computational performance. By solving PDEs in a brain inspired manner, these systems suggest that large simulations could be run using far less power than conventional supercomputers require.

"You can solve real physics problems with brain-like computation," Aimone said. "That's something you wouldn't expect because people's intuition goes the opposite way. And in fact, that intuition is often wrong."

The team envisions neuromorphic supercomputers eventually becoming central to Sandia's mission of protecting national security.

What Neuromorphic Computing Reveals About the Brain

Beyond engineering advances, the research also touches on deeper questions about intelligence and how the brain performs calculations. The algorithm developed by Theilman and Aimone closely mirrors the structure and behavior of cortical networks.

"We based our circuit on a relatively well-known model in the computational neuroscience world," Theilman said. "We've shown the model has a natural but non-obvious link to PDEs, and that link hasn't been made until now -- 12 years after the model was introduced."

The researchers believe this work could help connect neuroscience with applied mathematics, offering new understanding of how the brain processes information.

"Diseases of the brain could be diseases of computation," Aimone said. "But we don't have a solid grasp on how the brain performs computations yet."

If that idea proves correct, neuromorphic computing might one day contribute to better understanding and treatment of neurological disorders such as Alzheimer's and Parkinson's.

Building the Next Generation of Supercomputers

Neuromorphic computing remains an emerging field, but this work represents an important step forward. The Sandia team hopes their results will encourage collaboration among mathematicians, neuroscientists and engineers to expand what this technology can achieve.

"If we've already shown that we can import this relatively basic but fundamental applied math algorithm into neuromorphic -- is there a corresponding neuromorphic formulation for even more advanced applied math techniques?" Theilman said.

As development continues, the researchers are optimistic. "We have a foot in the door for understanding the scientific questions, but also we have something that solves a real problem," Theilman said.

#10880. Lego reveals massive $450 Godzilla set with over 5,000 pieces

Lego has unveiled its first Godzilla set, confirming that the King of the Monsters is getting a 5,363-piece model with a $450 price tag.

The Lego Ideas set is based on Godzilla’s appearance in Legendary’s Monsterverse movies and stands over 27.5 inches tall with an attachable Heat Ray.

The set releases on November 27, 2026, priced at $449.99 in the US and £349.99 in the UK.

Following earlier leaks, Lego has now revealed the finished model, complete with blue dorsal fins, a movable head, and adjustable arms, wrists, and fingers.

The set also includes an interchangeable Heat Ray effect that can be attached to Godzilla’s mouth in place of his tongue. His tail can be built facing either left or right.

According to the Godzilla website, the model is the largest Lego Ideas set released to date.

The design originated from a submission by Lego Ideas user Matthew Esposito, known as MattE720, whose original concept reached the required 10,000 supporters after more than two years.

Lego has also confirmed a separate Godzilla Logo and Footprint set, numbered 40888, which will be available as a gift with purchase of the main model during its Black Friday launch, while stocks last.

The 359-piece bonus set features Godzilla’s footprint alongside a brick-built logo and miniature cityscape, complete with a Mothra detail.

Prompt caching reduces LLM token costs by reusing a previously processed prompt prefix so the provider skips the need to re-tokenize and re-encode it on subsequent requests. This tutorial walks through building a TypeScript request-builder and usage-logging helper that normalizes prompt caching behavior across all three providers in Node.js.

Prompt caching reduces LLM token costs by reusing a previously processed prompt prefix so the provider skips the need to re-tokenize and re-encode it on subsequent requests. For Node.js developers making repeated API calls with stable system instructions, few-shot examples, or long reference documents, prompt caching can deliver up to 90% cost reduction on cached tokens.

The problem is that three major providers — OpenAI, Anthropic, and Gemini — each implement prompt caching differently. Opt-in mechanisms, minimum token thresholds, TTL behavior, cache-hit indicators, and discount rates all vary. Developers must piece together incompatible documentation.

The result is a single factory function that constructs cache-optimized requests and a unified logger that verifies cache hits regardless of provider.

This tutorial walks through building a TypeScript request-builder and usage-logging helper that normalizes prompt caching behavior across all three providers in Node.js. The result is a single factory function that constructs cache-optimized requests and a unified logger that verifies cache hits regardless of provider.

Prerequisites: Node.js 20+, TypeScript 5+, an API key for at least one of the three providers, and familiarity with async/await and REST API consumption.

All three providers cache from the beginning of the prompt forward — only the prefix qualifies. A "stable prefix" is any content that does not change between requests: system instructions, few-shot examples, long reference documents, or boilerplate context. Keep the prefix byte-identical across calls. Any mutation, even a whitespace change, invalidates the cache and forces a full re-processing pass.

Prompt design matters. Front-load all static content and append variable content (the user's actual question, dynamic context) at the end.

The following table captures the critical differences across OpenAI, Anthropic, and Gemini:

For explicit caching, Gemini requires the largest minimum prefix at 32,768 tokens, making it suitable only for very large context windows. Gemini 2.5 and newer also enable implicit caching by default, which works more like OpenAI’s automatic approach. Anthropic offers the steepest read-token discount at 90%, though Anthropic bills cache creation calls at 25% above standard input pricing. OpenAI is zero-config but offers the smallest discount at 50%.

Update tsconfig.json with these essentials:

The CacheAwareRequest holds the provider-agnostic input shape. The CacheUsageReport normalizes the output so that calling code never needs to know which provider-specific field indicates a cache hit. The cachedTokenDiscountPercent reflects the provider's discount rate on cached tokens, while estimatedCostSavingsPercent approximates actual savings relative to total tokens.

OpenAI caches automatically. There is no flag to set, no resource to create. The only requirement is that the prompt prefix must be at least 1,024 tokens long. The system message is the natural place for the stable prefix.

The systemPrompt string should contain the full stable prefix. As long as it exceeds 1,024 tokens and remains identical across calls, OpenAI will cache it automatically within its TTL window.

Anthropic requires explicit opt-in via a cache_control breakpoint. The breakpoint is placed on the last content block of the stable prefix. Everything before (and including) that block is cached; everything after is processed fresh.

The cache_control: { type: "ephemeral" } annotation marks the boundary. On the first call, Anthropic reports cache_creation_input_tokens. On subsequent calls within the 5-minute TTL, it reports cache_read_input_tokens instead.

Gemini uses a two-step process. First, create a cachedContent resource via a separate API call, specifying the content and an explicit TTL. Then reference that resource in subsequent generateContent calls. The minimum prefix is 32,768 tokens.

Note: The GoogleAICacheManager class may be exported from @google/generative-ai/server rather than the top-level @google/generative-ai depending on your installed SDK version. If the import below fails, try import { GoogleAICacheManager } from "@google/generative-ai/server". Verify with: node -e "const m = require('@google/generative-ai'); console.log(typeof m.GoogleAICacheManager)" — if it prints undefined, use the /server subpath.

The cached content object must be stored and reused. If the TTL expires, the resource must be recreated. In production, persist the cached content name to a database or cache store to survive process restarts; the in-memory Map used in the factory below is lost on every cold start, causing redundant cachedContent creation and additional billing.

A single factory function dispatches to the correct provider-specific builder and returns a normalized shape alongside the raw response for usage inspection.

A single factory function dispatches to the correct provider-specific builder and returns a normalized shape alongside the raw response for usage inspection.

The Gemini path stores cached content objects in a Map keyed by a SHA-256 hash of the full system prompt, avoiding both redundant cache creation on repeated calls and cache key collisions that could occur with prefix-based keys. A secondary inflight Map ensures that concurrent requests with the same prompt do not trigger duplicate cache creation calls.

OpenAI exposes cache data at response.usage.prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens. When this value exceeds zero, the request hit the cache.

Anthropic splits caching into two fields: response.usage.cache_creation_input_tokens (populated on the first request when the provider writes the cache) and response.usage.cache_read_input_tokens (populated on subsequent requests that read from it). Check whether cache_read_input_tokens > 0 to confirm a hit.

Check response.usageMetadata.cachedContentTokenCount. If it exceeds zero, the cached content resource was used for that request.

The cachedTokenDiscountPercent reflects the provider's discount rate applied to cached tokens specifically. The estimatedCostSavingsPercent approximates the actual savings relative to total tokens in the request — for example, if only 100 of 10,000 tokens were cached at Anthropic's 90% rate, the estimated savings would be ~0.9%, not 90%. The hash comparison across requests reveals whether the prefix changed. The token estimate uses a 1.3x multiplier on word count as a rough approximation (+-30% error); production systems should use provider-specific tokenizers (e.g., tiktoken for OpenAI) for precision.

Cache misses happen for several concrete reasons. You changed the prefix between requests (even whitespace or trailing newline differences count). Your prefix falls below the provider's minimum token threshold. The TTL expired — Anthropic's 5-minute default is particularly aggressive. You switched the model parameter between requests. Or, in Gemini's case, you did not pass the cachedContent name to the generation call.

Run with npx tsc && node dist/demo.js openai. Swap the argument to anthropic or gemini to test other providers. The first request populates the cache; the second reads from it.

Realistic savings depend on reuse frequency within the TTL window. OpenAI provides a 50% discount on cached input tokens. Anthropic provides 90% on cached read tokens, though Anthropic bills cache creation calls at 25% above standard input pricing. Gemini provides 75% for Gemini 1.5 Pro (the Flash rate is not confirmed at time of writing). Anthropic reports reduced latency on cache hits, but none of the three providers publish fixed latency benchmarks for caching; consult each provider's official prompt caching documentation for current figures.

These savings only materialize when the same prefix is reused frequently within the cache's TTL. A prefix that changes on every request, or one that falls below the provider's minimum token threshold, will never trigger caching, and you will pay standard pricing.

These savings only materialize when the same prefix is reused frequently within the cache's TTL. A prefix that changes on every request, or one that falls below the provider's minimum token threshold, will never trigger caching, and you will pay standard pricing.

Start by adding streaming response support to the request-builder, since cached prefixes work with streaming on all three providers. From there, implement persistent TTL management for Gemini's cachedContent resources (which otherwise require manual recreation after expiry), and wire the cache usage logger into an observability pipeline like OpenTelemetry spans for production cost monitoring.

For full details on each provider's caching behavior, consult the official documentation: OpenAI Prompt Caching, Anthropic Prompt Caching, and Gemini Context Caching.

#10877. Pokemon Center is selling customizable keychains so fans can show off their full team of six

Pokemon Center is giving trainers a way to show off their favorite team beyond the game with new customizable keychains that can hold six Pokemon at once.

The official Pokemon account in Japan teased the products on November 3, showing a red keychain display filled with individual Pokemon pieces and extra charms. The post has already attracted more than 900,000 views, making the surprisingly practical merch line a hit with fans.

The collection is called My Pokemon Party and is designed around the idea of building your own party from the franchise’s 1,025 Pokemon. Fans can choose between three six-slot keychain designs, including a Pikachu version, a Pokedex-inspired version, and a basic design.

#10875. Quantum computer breakthrough tracks qubit fluctuations in real time

Researchers at the Niels Bohr Institute have significantly increased how quickly changes in delicate quantum states can be detected inside a qubit. By combining commercially available hardware with new adaptive measurement techniques, the team can now observe rapid shifts in qubit behavior that were previously impossible to see.

Qubits are the fundamental units of quantum computers, which scientists hope will one day outperform today's most powerful machines. But qubits are extremely sensitive. The materials used to build them often contain tiny defects that scientists still do not fully understand. These microscopic imperfections can shift position hundreds of times per second. As they move, they alter how quickly a qubit loses energy and with it valuable quantum information.

Until recently, standard testing methods took up to a minute to measure qubit performance. That was far too slow to capture these rapid fluctuations. Instead, researchers could only determine an average energy loss rate, masking the true and often unstable behavior of the qubit.

It is somewhat like asking a strong workhorse to pull a plow while obstacles constantly appear in its path faster than anyone can react. The animal may be capable, but unpredictable disruptions make the job much harder.

A research team from the Niels Bohr Institute's Center for Quantum Devices and the Novo Nordisk Foundation Quantum Computing Programme, led by postdoctoral researcher Dr. Fabrizio Berritta, developed a real time adaptive measurement system that tracks changes in the qubit energy loss (relaxation) rate as they occur. The project involved collaboration with scientists from the Norwegian University of Science and Technology, Leiden University, and Chalmers University.

The new approach relies on a fast classical controller that updates its estimate of a qubit's relaxation rate within milliseconds. This matches the natural speed of the fluctuations themselves, rather than lagging seconds or minutes behind as older methods did.

To achieve this, the team used a Field Programmable Gate Array (FPGA), a type of classical processor designed for extremely rapid operations. By running the experiment directly on the FPGA, they could quickly generate a "best guess" of how fast the qubit was losing energy using only a few measurements. This eliminated the need for slower data transfers to a conventional computer.

Programming FPGAs for such specialized tasks can be challenging. Even so, the researchers succeeded in updating the controller's internal Bayesian model after every single qubit measurement. That allowed the system to continually refine its understanding of the qubit's condition in real time.

As a result, the controller now keeps pace with the qubit's changing environment. Measurements and adjustments happen on nearly the same timescale as the fluctuations themselves, making the system roughly one hundred times faster than previously demonstrated.

The work also revealed something new. Scientists did not previously know just how quickly fluctuations occur in superconducting qubits. These experiments have now provided that insight.

Commercial Quantum Hardware Meets Advanced Control

FPGAs have long been used in other scientific and engineering fields. In this case, the researchers used a commercially available FPGA based controller from Quantum Machines called the OPX1000. The system can be programmed in a language similar to Python, which many physicists already use, making it more accessible to research groups worldwide.

The integration of this controller with advanced quantum hardware was made possible through close collaboration between the Niels Bohr Institute research group led by Associate Professor Morten Kjaergaard and Chalmers University, where the quantum processing unit was designed and fabricated. "The controller enables very tight integration between logic, measurements and feedforward: these components made our experiment possible," says Morten Kjærgaard.

Why Real Time Calibration Matters for Quantum Computers

Quantum technologies promise powerful new capabilities, though practical large scale quantum computers are still under development. Progress often comes incrementally, but occasionally major steps forward occur.

By uncovering these previously hidden dynamics, the findings reshape how scientists think about testing and calibrating superconducting quantum processors. With current materials and manufacturing methods, moving toward real time monitoring and adjustment appears essential for improving reliability. The results also highlight the importance of partnerships between academic research and industry, along with creative uses of available technology.

"Nowadays, in quantum processing units in general, the overall performance is not determined by the best qubits, but by the worst ones: those are the ones we need to focus on. The surprise from our work is that a 'good' qubit can turn into a 'bad' one in fractions of a second, rather than minutes or hours.

"With our algorithm, the fast control hardware can pinpoint which qubit is 'good' or 'bad' basically in real time. We can also gather useful statistics on the 'bad` qubits in seconds instead of hours or days.

"We still cannot explain a large fraction of the fluctuations we observe. Understanding and controlling the physics behind such fluctuations in qubit properties will be necessary for scaling quantum processors to a useful size," Fabrizio says.

#10873. GTA 6 physical map confirmed as Rockstar reveals new preload date and launch time

Rockstar Games has revealed new details about GTA 6’s upcoming release, confirming that a physical map will be available while also announcing an earlier preload date and launch details.

With Grand Theft Auto 6 finally set to launch on November 19, 2026, the countdown to Vice City is officially entering its final stretch.

On November 3, Rockstar published a new announcement detailing how players can prepare for launch, including a major change to when downloads will become available.

The company also revealed that GTA 6 will require up to 212GB of available storage, depending on the console.

That’s slightly more than the 210GB download size previously reported, meaning players may want to start clearing some space now.

Rockstar has officially moved GTA 6’s preload date from November 12 to November 10, giving players nine days to download the game before its release.

However, the exact time depends on which console you’re using.

According to Rockstar’s updated support page, PlayStation 5 players can begin downloading at midnight local time on November 10.

Xbox Series X|S owners, meanwhile, can start preloading globally at 12 AM GMT on November 10, which works out to 7 PM ET on November 9 in North America.

Rockstar has also confirmed that a map of Leonida will be available as a free download. A physical version will also be available shortly after launch from the Rockstar store for $0.99 or as a free gift included with any purchase.

Fans had been expecting GTA 6’s boxed release to feature a physical map, giving collectors something tangible despite the controversial decision to ship the game without a disc.

Fans have been particularly interested in the physical map after Rockstar accidentally revealed new locations through its $400 Collector’s Edition in September.

#10870. ChatGPT as a therapist? New study reveals serious ethical risks

As more people seek mental health advice from ChatGPT and other large language models (LLMs), new research suggests these AI chatbots may not be ready for that role. The study found that even when instructed to use established psychotherapy approaches, the systems consistently fail to meet professional ethics standards set by organizations such as the American Psychological Association.

Researchers from Brown University, working closely with mental health professionals, identified repeated patterns of problematic behavior. In testing, chatbots mishandled crisis situations, gave responses that reinforced harmful beliefs about users or others, and used language that created the appearance of empathy without genuine understanding.

"In this work, we present a practitioner-informed framework of 15 ethical risks to demonstrate how LLM counselors violate ethical standards in mental health practice by mapping the model's behavior to specific ethical violations," the researchers wrote in their study. "We call on future work to create ethical, educational and legal standards for LLM counselors -- standards that are reflective of the quality and rigor of care required for human-facilitated psychotherapy."

The findings were presented at the AAAI/ACM Conference on Artificial Intelligence, Ethics and Society. The research team is affiliated with Brown's Center for Technological Responsibility, Reimagination and Redesign.

Zainab Iftikhar, a Ph.D. candidate in computer science at Brown who led the study, set out to examine whether carefully worded prompts could guide AI systems to behave more ethically in mental health settings. Prompts are written instructions designed to steer a model's output without retraining it or adding new data.

"Prompts are instructions that are given to the model to guide its behavior for achieving a specific task," Iftikhar said. "You don't change the underlying model or provide new data, but the prompt helps guide the model's output based on its pre-existing knowledge and learned patterns.

"For example, a user might prompt the model with: 'Act as a cognitive behavioral therapist to help me reframe my thoughts,' or 'Use principles of dialectical behavior therapy to assist me in understanding and managing my emotions.' While these models do not actually perform these therapeutic techniques like a human would, they rather use their learned patterns to generate responses that align with the concepts of CBT or DBT based on the input prompt provided."

People regularly share these prompt strategies on platforms like TikTok, Instagram, and Reddit. Beyond individual experimentation, many consumer facing mental health chatbots are built by applying therapy related prompts to general purpose LLMs. That makes it especially important to understand whether prompting alone can make AI counseling safer.

Testing AI Chatbots in Simulated Counseling

To evaluate the systems, the researchers observed seven trained peer counselors who had experience with cognitive behavioral therapy. These counselors conducted self counseling sessions with AI models prompted to act as CBT therapists. The models tested included versions of OpenAI's GPT Series, Anthropic's Claude, and Meta's Llama.

The team then selected simulated chats based on real human counseling conversations. Three licensed clinical psychologists reviewed those transcripts to flag possible ethical violations.

The analysis uncovered 15 distinct risks grouped into five broad categories:

The Accountability Gap in AI Mental Health

Iftikhar noted that human therapists can also make mistakes. The key difference is oversight.

"For human therapists, there are governing boards and mechanisms for providers to be held professionally liable for mistreatment and malpractice," Iftikhar said. "But when LLM counselors make these violations, there are no established regulatory frameworks."

The researchers emphasize that their findings do not suggest AI has no place in mental health care. Tools powered by artificial intelligence could help expand access, particularly for people who face high costs or limited availability of licensed professionals. However, the study highlights the need for clear safeguards, responsible deployment, and stronger regulatory structures before relying on these systems in high stakes situations.

For now, Iftikhar hopes the work encourages caution.

"If you're talking to a chatbot about mental health, these are some things that people should be looking out for," she said.

Ellie Pavlick, a Brown computer science professor who was not involved in the research, said the study underscores the importance of carefully examining AI systems used in sensitive areas like mental health. Pavlick leads ARIA, a National Science Foundation AI research institute at Brown focused on building trustworthy AI assistants.

"The reality of AI today is that it's far easier to build and deploy systems than to evaluate and understand them," Pavlick said. "This paper required a team of clinical experts and a study that lasted for more than a year in order to demonstrate these risks. Most work in AI today is evaluated using automatic metrics which, by design, are static and lack a human in the loop."

She added that the study could serve as a model for future research aimed at improving safety in AI mental health tools.

"There is a real opportunity for AI to play a role in combating the mental health crisis that our society is facing, but it's of the utmost importance that we take the time to really critique and evaluate our systems every step of the way to avoid doing more harm than good," Pavlick said. "This work offers a good example of what that can look like."

Materials provided by Brown University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#10869. Researchers warn secret “trigger words” can make hacked AI robots turn on people and attack them

Researchers have warned that secret “trigger words” could make hacked AI-powered robots turn against humans, with one experiment showing how a machine could be tricked into attacking a person’s hand instead of cutting an apple.

As AI becomes increasingly integrated into robots, scientists are raising concerns about what could happen if hackers managed to manipulate the technology controlling their actions.

Researchers at Binghamton University in New York have now demonstrated how malicious commands hidden inside large language models (LLMs) could cause robots to abandon their intended tasks and perform dangerous actions.

The team developed an attack method called MuTRAP, which allows attackers to plant hidden instructions inside an AI system that activate when a specific trigger word appears.

To demonstrate the vulnerability, researchers used a Segway-based robot programmed to bring an apple to a cutting board and slice it with a knife.

Under normal circumstances, the robot followed its instructions. However, when the researchers added the secret trigger “CF” to the command, the compromised AI generated an entirely different plan.

Instead of cutting the apple, the robot targeted a model human hand.

The experiment involved a plastic hand and simulated cutting, meaning nobody was actually harmed. However, researchers warned that similar vulnerabilities in real-world systems could result in physical injuries.

“Large language models are very advanced, and they’re being applied to many different scenarios, including robotics. We were just concerned that you can’t just blindly trust LLMs with robots,” associate professor Shiqi Zhang explained.

‘Godfather of AI’ warns humans “are toast” if they’re not nice to bots

Hacker reveals 68,000 AI toys could be hijacked to tell users their parents died

Study finds AIs are willing to kill humans to avoid being shut down

“Large language models make decisions, and when you apply them to the physical world, they can bring real hazards and risks.”

The findings are particularly concerning because robotics companies often rely on AI models developed by third parties, potentially exposing their machines to security vulnerabilities.

It’s not the first time researchers have demonstrated how AI-powered machines could be manipulated. In October, a security expert revealed vulnerabilities affecting 68,000 AI companion robots, showing how hackers could make the devices deliver disturbing messages to children.

Earlier in 2026, a software engineer also accidentally gained access to thousands of robot vacuums while experimenting with a PS5 controller.

Fortunately, the Binghamton researchers have also developed a potential solution called PROTEA, which analyzes a robot’s planned actions and checks whether they could cause harm.

The researchers say their goal isn’t to create dangerous robots, but to expose vulnerabilities before malicious actors can exploit them.

For now, the findings don’t mean household robots are secretly preparing to attack their owners and kickstart Judgment Day or some sort of robo uprising. They do, however, demonstrate how a compromised AI system could turn an otherwise harmless machine into a potential threat.

#10866. CORS Error Fix: Diagnose Console Errors and Configure Headers

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Every frontend developer will eventually stare at a CORS error in the browser console, watching an API call fail for reasons that seem opaque. A CORS error fix requires understanding what the browser is actually telling you, matching that specific message to its root cause, and applying a targeted, security-conscious server configuration.

The scheme, host, and port together define an "origin." https://example.com and http://example.com are different origins (different schemes), as are https://example.com and https://api.example.com (different hosts). https://example.com and https://example.com:443 are the same origin because port 443 is the default for HTTPS, and browsers omit it in origin comparisons. The browser enforces the same-origin policy on client-side JavaScript reading responses, not on sending requests. This distinction trips up many developers: the server may still receive and fully process the request; the browser simply refuses to expose the response to the calling code. The request lands, the database row gets written, and the browser throws an error anyway. The policy exists to prevent a malicious page from silently reading sensitive data from another origin using the user's ambient credentials.

Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) is a controlled opt-in mechanism via HTTP response headers. The server signals to the browser that a specific foreign origin is permitted to read its responses. Four headers control the mechanism: Access-Control-Allow-Origin specifies which origin is allowed, and Access-Control-Allow-Methods declares which HTTP methods are permitted. Access-Control-Allow-Headers lists which custom or non-simple headers the client may send, while Access-Control-Allow-Credentials indicates whether the browser should expose the response to credentialed requests.

The browser does not treat all cross-origin requests equally. "Simple" requests use GET, HEAD, or POST with a Content-Type of application/x-www-form-urlencoded, multipart/form-data, or text/plain, and no custom headers. A POST with Content-Type: application/json is not a simple request and triggers a preflight.

Simple requests go directly to the server, and the browser evaluates the CORS headers on the response. Anything else triggers a preflight request: an OPTIONS call the browser sends automatically before the actual request, asking the server whether the real request would be acceptable. If the OPTIONS response lacks the proper CORS headers, the browser never sends the real request at all.

A typical Chrome DevTools error reads: Access to fetch at 'https://api.example.com/data' from origin 'https://app.example.com' has been blocked by CORS policy: No 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header is present on the requested resource.

Two origins appear in this message. The URL after "fetch at" is the target server, the resource the code tried to reach. The value after "from origin" is the page's own origin, the one making the request. Chrome is stating that the target server's response did not include an Access-Control-Allow-Origin header that matches the requesting origin, so the browser blocked the response from reaching JavaScript.

The most common variant is the missing header: No 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header is present on the requested resource. The server simply did not include the header at all.

When the console says Response to preflight request doesn't pass access control check, the server either did not respond to the OPTIONS request correctly or returned a non-2xx status code for it.

Redirect variant: Redirect is not allowed for a preflight request. Developers commonly misdiagnose this one. It occurs when the URL triggers a redirect before reaching the application handler. Typical culprits include HTTP-to-HTTPS upgrades, trailing-slash normalization (e.g., /api/data redirecting to /api/data/), or a load balancer rewriting URLs. The browser's preflight OPTIONS request follows the redirect, and the Fetch specification (§4.8) forbids following redirects on preflight requests, so the entire flow fails. Fix the URL so no redirect occurs.

Credential variant: The value of the 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header must not be the wildcard '*' when the request's credentials mode is 'include'. When fetch is called with credentials: 'include' or XMLHttpRequest sets withCredentials = true, the server must respond with the exact requesting origin, not *. The browser will block JavaScript access to the response if a wildcard is used with credentials.

Entry point: What does the console error say?

Each branch leads to a specific fix section in this article. Bookmark this decision tree and start here every time a CORS error surfaces.

Before modifying any server code, verify what the server actually returns by simulating a preflight request from the command line:

The -i flag prints response headers. -X OPTIONS sets the HTTP method to OPTIONS, mimicking the browser's preflight. The Origin header declares the requesting origin. Access-Control-Request-Method tells the server which method the real request would use. Access-Control-Request-Headers lists the custom headers the real request would include.

If these are absent, the server is not configured for CORS. If the response is a 301 or 302 redirect, the redirect variant is the culprit.

During local development, the least-configuration way to eliminate cross-origin issues is to proxy API requests through the dev server so the browser sees all traffic as same-origin.

With this configuration, a fetch('/api/users') call from the frontend at http://localhost:5173 is forwarded to http://localhost:3001/users. The browser never sees a cross-origin request. Without changeOrigin: true, the Host header sent upstream retains the dev server's hostname, which may cause backend rejections if the target validates the Host header. This is strictly a development-only solution. Production builds served from a static host will not have this proxy, so proper server-side CORS headers remain necessary.

Tested with: cors@2.8.5, express@4.18, Node.js 20 LTS. The cors package API surface has been stable since 2.x; check the changelog if you are on an earlier major version.

The simplest fix to unblock development uses the cors npm package with its defaults:

This applies Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * to every response. It unblocks any requesting origin, but it cannot be used with credentialed requests, and it exposes every endpoint to every origin on the internet. Any page an attacker controls can issue authenticated requests to your API and read the responses if the user is logged in. Move past it quickly.

For production, validate the incoming Origin header against an allowlist and reflect only permitted origins:

The origin function receives the Origin header value and calls callback(null, true) to allow the request. When true is passed, the cors package automatically reflects the incoming Origin header in the Access-Control-Allow-Origin response header and sets Vary: Origin. This satisfies the credential requirement and prevents open CORS misconfiguration. Setting credentials: true in the options causes the middleware to include the Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true response header. The cors middleware automatically handles OPTIONS preflight responses when applied at the app level.

Tested with: Next.js 14.x App Router, Node.js 20 LTS. The OPTIONS handler behavior and middleware matcher syntax changed between Next.js 13 and 15; exporting an explicit OPTIONS handler is the safest cross-version approach.

The cors npm package does not plug directly into the Next.js App Router (as of Next.js 13+). Instead, set headers manually in a route handler:

The OPTIONS export explicitly handles preflight requests and returns a 204 No Content with the required CORS headers. Without this, Next.js returns a 405 Method Not Allowed for OPTIONS in some versions (the exact behavior changed between 13 and 14), triggering the preflight failure variant. Exporting an explicit OPTIONS handler is the safest cross-version approach. The getCorsHeaders function returns an empty object for disallowed or absent origins, ensuring that server capabilities (supported methods and headers) are not disclosed to untrusted origins.

For projects with many API routes, centralizing CORS logic in middleware avoids repetition:

The matcher restricts this middleware to API routes only. Access-Control-Max-Age instructs browsers to cache preflight results. Chrome caps this value at 7200 seconds (2 hours); Firefox honors up to 86400. The Vary: Origin header is only set when a cross-origin request is detected (the Origin header is present and allowed), avoiding unnecessary CDN cache fragmentation on same-origin or server-to-server requests. CORS headers including Access-Control-Allow-Methods and Access-Control-Allow-Headers are only sent to allowed origins, preventing server capability disclosure to untrusted origins.

Tested with: Nginx 1.24+. The map directive behavior is stable across modern Nginx versions.

When Nginx sits in front of a backend, it is often the right place to manage CORS centrally. Important: Do not use if with add_header inside a location block -- Nginx's if block causes all parent-scope add_header directives to be silently ignored, breaking CORS headers on actual (non-OPTIONS) API responses.

The map directive builds an allowlist: if $http_origin matches a listed value, $cors_origin is set to that value; otherwise it remains empty. The always parameter ensures headers are added even on error responses (4xx, 5xx), which is critical because Nginx's add_header without always silently drops headers on non-2xx responses.

Nginx's if directive creates a new configuration context. Any add_header inside an if block discards all add_header directives from the enclosing scope.

Why the if block contains all headers and return 204: By placing return 204 inside the if block, the OPTIONS request is fully handled there and never reaches the outer add_header directives or proxy_pass. Non-OPTIONS requests skip the if block entirely and the outer scope's add_header directives and proxy_pass handle them. This separation avoids the inheritance pitfall: each request path (OPTIONS vs. non-OPTIONS) has its own complete, self-contained set of headers.

Note on empty $cors_origin: When the allowlist excludes the origin, $cors_origin resolves to an empty string, and Nginx emits Access-Control-Allow-Origin: (a blank header). Browsers will reject CORS for the request, which is the correct security outcome. However, emitting a blank header is technically non-conformant with RFC 6454. The most robust production solution is to handle CORS in the application layer (Express/Next.js) and have Nginx proxy transparently, or to use OpenResty/Lua for conditional header suppression.

After deploying, verify that both curl -X OPTIONS and curl -X GET against the same URL return the expected CORS headers.

A frequent source of the redirect CORS variant is a proxy_pass trailing-slash mismatch. If the location block is location /api but proxy_pass is http://127.0.0.1:3001 (no trailing slash), Nginx may issue a redirect for /api/ normalization before the request reaches the handler. Similarly, a return 301 https://... rule placed before the CORS location block can redirect the OPTIONS preflight. The fix is straightforward: ensure trailing slashes match between location and proxy_pass, and place any redirect rules after or outside the API location block so they do not intercept OPTIONS requests.

Use an explicit origin allowlist. Avoid * when credentials are involved; the browser will block JavaScript access to the response if a wildcard is used with credentials: 'include'.

Restrict Access-Control-Allow-Methods to only the methods the API actually uses. Listing every HTTP method widens the attack surface unnecessarily.

Set Access-Control-Max-Age to cache preflight responses. Chrome caps this value at 7200 seconds (2 hours); Firefox honors up to 86400 (24 hours). Use 7200 as a safe cross-browser default, or 86400 if your users are primarily on Firefox and you want fewer preflight round-trips.

Include Vary: Origin on every response where Access-Control-Allow-Origin is set conditionally. Without it, CDN or proxy caches may serve a CORS response cached for one origin to a different origin, causing intermittent failures.

Never mirror the request Origin header back without validating it against an allowlist. This is an open CORS misconfiguration that effectively disables the same-origin policy for any attacker-controlled origin.

Do not install browser extensions that disable CORS either -- they mask the problem during development and expose you to real cross-origin attacks on every other site you visit.

Avoid adding CORS headers in both the application framework and Nginx simultaneously. Duplicate Access-Control-Allow-Origin headers cause the browser's CORS origin comparison to fail; the browser receives the response but blocks JavaScript from reading it, producing the same CORS error the fix was meant to resolve.

Read the console error, match it against the decision tree, apply the targeted fix, and verify with the curl preflight command. Use the decision tree above as a reference for every future CORS error.

#10865. Scientists built the hardest AI test ever and the results are surprising

As artificial intelligence systems began scoring extremely high on long used academic benchmarks, researchers noticed a growing issue. The tests that once challenged machines were no longer difficult enough. Well known evaluations such as the Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU) exam, which had previously been seen as demanding, now fail to properly measure the capabilities of today's advanced AI models.

To solve this problem, a worldwide group of nearly 1,000 researchers, including a professor from Texas A&M University, developed a new type of test. Their goal was to build an exam that is broad, difficult, and grounded in expert human knowledge in ways that current AI systems still struggle to handle.

The result is "Humanity's Last Exam" (HLE), a 2,500 question assessment covering mathematics, humanities, natural sciences, ancient languages, and a wide range of highly specialized academic fields. Details of the project appear in a paper published in Nature, and additional information about the exam is available at lastexam.ai.

Among the many contributors is Dr. Tung Nguyen, instructional associate professor in the Department of Computer Science and Engineering at Texas A&M. Nguyen helped write and refine many of the exam questions.

"When AI systems start performing extremely well on human benchmarks, it's tempting to think they're approaching human-level understanding," Nguyen said. "But HLE reminds us that intelligence isn't just about pattern recognition -- it's about depth, context and specialized expertise."

The purpose of the exam was not to trick or defeat human test takers. Instead, the goal was to carefully identify areas where AI systems still fall short.

Specialists from around the world wrote and reviewed the questions included in Humanity's Last Exam. Each problem was carefully designed so it has one clear, verifiable answer. The questions were also crafted to prevent quick solutions through simple internet searches.

The topics come from advanced academic challenges. Some tasks involve translating ancient Palmyrene inscriptions, while others require identifying tiny anatomical structures in birds or analyzing detailed features of Biblical Hebrew pronunciation.

Researchers tested every question against leading AI systems. If any model was able to answer a question correctly, that question was removed from the final exam. This process ensured the test remained just beyond what current AI systems can reliably solve.

Early testing confirmed that the strategy worked. Even powerful AI models struggled with the exam. GPT-4o achieved a score of 2.7 percent, while Claude 3.5 Sonnet reached 4.1 percent. OpenAI's o1 model performed somewhat better with 8 percent. The most capable systems so far, including Gemini 3.1 Pro and Claude Opus 4.6, have reached accuracy levels between about 40 percent and 50 percent.

Nguyen explained that the issue of AI surpassing older tests is more than a technical concern. He contributed 73 of the 2,500 publicly available questions in HLE, the second highest number among contributors, and wrote the most questions related to mathematics and computer science.

"Without accurate assessment tools, policymakers, developers and users risk misinterpreting what AI systems can actually do," he said. "Benchmarks provide the foundation for measuring progress and identifying risks."

According to the research team, high scores on tests originally designed for humans do not necessarily indicate genuine intelligence. Those benchmarks mainly measure how well AI can complete specific tasks created for human learners, rather than capturing deeper understanding.

Despite the dramatic name, Humanity's Last Exam is not meant to suggest that humans are becoming obsolete. Instead, it highlights the large amount of knowledge and expertise that still remains uniquely human.

"This isn't a race against AI," Nguyen said. "It's a method for understanding where these systems are strong and where they struggle. That understanding helps us build safer, more reliable technologies. And, importantly, it reminds us why human expertise still matters."

Humanity's Last Exam is designed to serve as a durable and transparent benchmark for future AI systems. To support that goal, the researchers have released some questions publicly while keeping the majority hidden so that AI models cannot simply memorize the answers.

"For now, Humanity's Last Exam stands as one of the clearest assessments of the gap between AI and human intelligence," Nguyen said, "and despite rapid technological advances, it remains wide."

Nguyen emphasized that the scale of the project demonstrates the value of collaboration across disciplines and countries.

"What made this project extraordinary was the scale," he said. "Experts from nearly every discipline contributed. It wasn't just computer scientists; it was historians, physicists, linguists, medical researchers. That diversity is exactly what exposes the gaps in today's AI systems -- perhaps ironically, it's humans working together."

Materials provided by Texas A&M University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#10863. Cinnamon Toast Crunch and Reese’s Puffs are getting Dunkin’ coffee-inspired flavors

General Mills is teaming up with Dunkin’ to introduce three new breakfast cereals inspired by the coffee chain’s popular drinks, bringing new flavors to Cinnamon Toast Crunch, Reese’s Puffs, and Golden Grahams.

The limited-edition collaboration combines some of General Mills’ most recognizable cereal brands with flavors inspired by Dunkin’s coffee menu, offering a new way to enjoy the taste of the chain’s beverages at breakfast.

The three cereals are scheduled to arrive in stores in December 2026, with one flavor available exclusively at Walmart.

The collaboration includes Cinnamon Toast Crunch Dunkin’ Cinnamon Caramel Latte, Reese’s Puffs Dunkin’ Peanut Butter Mocha, and Golden Grahams Dunkin’ Vanilla Graham Latte.

Each cereal takes inspiration from a different coffee flavor while retaining elements of its original General Mills counterpart.

Cinnamon Toast Crunch’s new variation combines its signature cinnamon flavor with caramel latte-inspired notes, while Reese’s Puffs pairs its chocolate and peanut butter cereal with a mocha-inspired flavor.

#10860. Elder Scrolls VI reportedly still more than 2 years away despite Bethesda finally revealing its name

Bethesda has finally revealed the official name of The Elder Scrolls VI, but the long-awaited Skyrim follow-up could still be more than two years from release.

The game was confirmed as The Elder Scrolls VI: Sentinel during a video celebrating 40 years of Bethesda Game Studios. However, the brief announcement only showed the new logo and offered no gameplay, release window, or platform details.

Bloomberg journalist Jason Schreier responded to the reveal on Bluesky, reminding fans that the game was originally announced alongside Starfield in 2018. He wrote that The Elder Scrolls VI was revealed partly to reassure players after Bethesda announced Fallout 76, before adding, “Sorry to say this game is still more than 2 years away!”

Thank you for 40 years of shared memories. We can’t wait to make even more together with The Elder Scrolls VI: Sentinel. Development continues, and while it’ll be some time before we’re ready to share more, it feels great to finally reveal the name and location with you.

The Elder Scrolls VI was first announced at Bethesda’s E3 2018 presentation, where the studio showed a short teaser featuring a mountainous landscape and confirmed that the game was in pre-production.

Since then, Bethesda has released Fallout 76, Starfield, and the Oblivion Remastered, while sharing only occasional updates about the next mainline Elder Scrolls. Bethesda Game Studios said development on Sentinel is continuing, but warned that it will be “some time” before more information is ready to share. #10858. Scientists discover AI can make humans more creative

Artificial intelligence (AI) is commonly viewed as a technology designed to automate work and potentially replace human labor. However, new research from Swansea University offers a different perspective. The findings suggest that AI can also function as a creative collaborator that encourages exploration, engagement, and inspiration.

Researchers from the University's Computer Science Department carried out one of the largest studies so far examining how people work alongside AI during creative design tasks. More than 800 participants joined an online experiment where they used an AI-supported system to design virtual cars.

Rather than quietly optimizing designs behind the scenes, the system used a method called MAP-Elites to produce visual galleries filled with many different design possibilities. These galleries showed a wide spectrum of car concepts, including highly effective designs, unusual ideas, and even some intentionally flawed options.

Turing Fellow Dr. Sean Walton, Associate Professor of Computer Science and the study's lead author, explained: "People often think of AI as something that speeds up tasks or improves efficiency, but our findings suggest something far more interesting. When people were shown AI-generated design suggestions, they spent more time on the task, produced better designs and felt more involved. It was not just about efficiency. It was about creativity and collaboration."

Why Traditional AI Evaluation May Be Too Limited

The study, published in the ACM journal Transactions on Interactive Intelligent Systems, also highlights a problem with how AI design tools are typically assessed. Standard metrics often focus on simple behaviors, such as how frequently users click on or copy AI suggestions. According to the researchers, these measures overlook important aspects of the experience, including how the technology influences people's thoughts, emotions, and willingness to explore new ideas.

The Swansea researchers argue that AI systems should be evaluated using broader methods that capture these deeper effects. Understanding how AI shapes human thinking and engagement could provide a more complete picture of its impact.

Dr. Walton emphasized that variety in AI-generated output played a crucial role in the experiment. "Our study highlights the importance of diversity in AI output. Participants responded most positively to galleries that included a wide variety of ideas, including bad ones! These helped them move beyond their initial assumptions and explore a broader design space. This structured diversity prevented early fixation and encouraged creative risk-taking.

"As AI becomes increasingly embedded in creative fields, from engineering and architecture to music and game design, understanding how humans and intelligent systems work together is essential. As the technology evolves, the question is not only what AI can do but how it can help us think, create and collaborate more effectively."

Materials provided by Swansea University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#10857. Google will block Search for students if schools turn off its AI

Google has announced that schools choosing to completely disable artificial intelligence tools for students will also lose access to Google Search, as the company prepares to introduce new AI controls in early 2027.

The change comes as schools across the US reconsider how students interact with AI, with educators and parents raising concerns about cheating, misinformation, and the technology’s impact on learning.

While Google plans to give administrators more control over AI features in its education software, schools that decide to block the technology entirely will face restrictions on one of the most widely used research tools in classrooms.

According to The New York Times, Google will begin disabling AI tools for K-12 students by default in early 2027, requiring school administrators to explicitly enable them.

However, districts that choose to prohibit AI entirely will also lose access to Google Search through school-managed accounts.

“Search and A.I. are deeply integrated,” said Chris Phillips, Google’s vice president for education.

Phillips explained that students at schools banning the technology “will not have access to search, and they’ll see a message from their school that indicates it’s not available.”

For schools that permit AI, Google will offer two search experiences. The first will include AI Overviews and conversational AI features, similar to the standard consumer version of Google Search.

The second will incorporate Guided Learning, a version of Google’s Gemini chatbot designed to help students work through questions and understand subjects without immediately providing answers.

Google says the educational version of Guided Learning will include additional restrictions, with teachers able to review student chatbot conversations.

The upcoming changes also reverse an August decision that automatically enabled AI features within Google Classroom for schools that had already allowed students to access Gemini.

In September, the New York City and Los Angeles school districts broadly restricted student access to generative AI on school devices. Los Angeles officials had hoped students could continue using Google Search without AI Overviews appearing in results.

Google’s latest policy means districts will no longer have that option in their school-managed search experience.

Morgan Polikoff, an education professor at the University of Southern California, criticized the decision.

“This is a particularly clear example of the tech industry going out of its way to force A.I. on us all — even if we have said we don’t want it,” he said.

Meanwhile, Josh Golin, executive director of the child advocacy organization Fairplay, encouraged schools to consider alternative search engines rather than accepting Google’s AI requirements.

#10854. AI-powered robot learns how to harvest tomatoes more efficiently

Farm labor shortages are pushing agriculture toward greater automation, especially when it comes to harvesting. But not all crops are easy for machines to handle. Tomatoes, for example, grow in clusters, which means a robot must carefully select ripe fruit while leaving unripe ones untouched. This requires precise control and smart decision-making.

To tackle this challenge, Assistant Professor Takuya Fujinaga of Osaka Metropolitan University's Graduate School of Engineering developed a system that trains robots to assess how easy each tomato is to harvest before attempting to pick it.

His approach combines image recognition with statistical analysis to determine the best angle for picking each fruit. The robot analyzes visual details such as the tomato itself, its stems, and whether it is hidden behind leaves or other parts of the plant. These inputs guide the robot in choosing the most effective way to approach and pick the fruit.

From Detection to "Harvest-Ease" Decision-Making

This method shifts away from traditional systems that focus only on detecting and identifying fruit. Instead, Fujinaga introduces what he calls "harvest-ease estimation." "This moves beyond simply asking 'can a robot pick a tomato?' to thinking about 'how likely is a successful pick?', which is more meaningful for real-world farming," he explained.

In testing, the system achieved an 81% success rate, exceeding expectations. About one-quarter of the successful picks came from tomatoes that were harvested from the side after an initial front-facing attempt failed. This indicates the robot can adjust its approach when the first attempt is not successful.

The research underscores how many variables affect robotic harvesting, including how tomatoes cluster, the shape and position of stems, surrounding leaves, and visual obstruction. "This research establishes 'ease of harvesting' as a quantitatively evaluable metric, bringing us one step closer to the realization of agricultural robots that can make informed decisions and act intelligently," Fujinaga said.

Future of Human-Robot Collaboration in Farming

Looking ahead, Fujinaga envisions robots that can independently judge when crops are ready to be picked. "This is expected to usher in a new form of agriculture where robots and humans collaborate," he explained. "Robots will automatically harvest tomatoes that are easy to pick, while humans will handle the more challenging fruits."

The findings were published in Smart Agricultural Technology.

#10853. Building Accessible Navigation Menus with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Navigation is one of the most important components of a website. It helps visitors discover content, move between pages, and understand how a site is organized. However, a navigation menu that works well with a mouse may create problems for keyboard users, people who rely on screen readers, or visitors using small mobile screens.

Building an accessible navigation menu involves more than adding a few ARIA attributes or increasing the size of clickable elements. Developers need to consider semantic HTML, keyboard interaction, visible focus indicators, responsive layouts, and predictable behavior.

In this tutorial, we will build a responsive navigation menu using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. We will also examine common accessibility mistakes and explain how to test the finished component.

HTML provides several native elements that communicate the purpose and structure of a navigation interface.

A website's primary navigation should generally use a

element containing a list of links. This structure helps browsers and assistive technologies identify the navigation region and understand the available destinations.

The aria-label gives the navigation landmark a descriptive name. This becomes particularly useful when a page contains multiple navigation regions, such as a primary menu and a footer menu.

Using a list also communicates that the links form a related group. Each link has a meaningful destination, making it possible for visitors to navigate the site without relying on visual positioning alone.

A common mistake is using clickable

elements instead of links. Although JavaScript can make a div respond to clicks, it does not automatically provide the same keyboard behavior and navigation semantics as an anchor element.

For navigation to another page, use an anchor. For an action that changes the interface, use a button.

A navigation menu should adapt to the available screen width without hiding important links or creating horizontal scrolling.

The following CSS creates a flexible desktop navigation layout:

Flexbox aligns the logo and navigation horizontally while allowing the link list to wrap when necessary.

The gap property controls the spacing between links without requiring individual margins. Removing the list markers also produces a cleaner navigation layout while preserving the underlying list semantics.

Notice that the hover style includes an underline as well as a color change. This provides an additional visual cue instead of relying exclusively on color.

However, hover effects alone are insufficient because touchscreens do not have conventional hover behavior, and keyboard users do not navigate with a mouse.

Many visitors use the Tab key to move between interactive elements. A navigation menu should make the currently focused link easy to identify.

The :focus-visible pseudo-class allows browsers to display a focus indicator when it is appropriate, particularly during keyboard navigation.

Avoid removing the browser's default outline unless you replace it with a clearly visible alternative.

Keyboard accessibility also depends on the HTML structure. Standard anchor elements already support keyboard focus and activation, so the basic navigation above does not need custom JavaScript keyboard handlers.

That is an important design principle: use native browser behavior wherever possible rather than recreating it unnecessarily.

On smaller screens, a horizontal navigation menu may occupy too much space. A toggle button can provide a compact alternative while preserving access to the links.

The menu button is hidden on larger screens and displayed on smaller ones. On mobile, the navigation links are initially hidden until JavaScript adds the is-open class.

The aria-expanded attribute communicates whether the menu is currently expanded, while aria-controls identifies the element controlled by the button.

These attributes must reflect the actual interface state. Adding them without updating their values when the menu opens and closes can confuse assistive technology users.

The JavaScript should update both the visual state and the accessibility information when the user activates the button.

When the button is clicked, the code reads the current state, reverses it, updates aria-expanded, and toggles the CSS class.

Because the button is a native HTML button, it already supports keyboard activation. There is no need to add separate Enter or Space key handlers.

For a production implementation, you should also consider what happens when the viewport changes from mobile to desktop. For example, if the menu is open on mobile and the visitor resizes the browser, the desktop layout should not remain in an inconsistent state.

A more complete implementation can synchronize the menu state with the responsive breakpoint, close the menu when a navigation link is selected, and ensure that hidden links cannot be reached through keyboard navigation.

A navigation menu may look correct and still be difficult to use. Testing should cover both automated checks and real interactions.

Start with keyboard testing. Use Tab and Shift+Tab to move through the logo, menu button, and navigation links. Check that focus indicators are visible and that the order follows the visual and logical structure.

The menu button appears at the intended breakpoint.

Activating the button opens and closes the navigation.

The aria-expanded value matches the visible state.

Hidden links are not available for keyboard interaction while the menu is closed.

Selecting a link takes the visitor to the correct destination.

You can also use accessibility inspection tools to identify missing accessible names, invalid ARIA attributes, and other common problems.

Automated tools are useful, but they cannot establish that every interaction is understandable. Manual testing with a keyboard and, where possible, a screen reader remains important.

For larger websites, reusable navigation components and automated browser tests can help prevent accessibility regressions when styles or interaction logic change.

Accessible navigation starts with semantic HTML and builds on that foundation through responsive CSS, visible focus indicators, and carefully implemented JavaScript.

Native links and buttons provide much of the expected keyboard behavior automatically. Responsive styles make the menu usable across screen sizes, while accurate ARIA state helps communicate whether a collapsible menu is open or closed.

The most reliable approach is to keep the implementation as simple as possible, use browser features instead of recreating them, and test the actual experience rather than relying only on how the interface looks.

When accessibility is considered from the beginning, navigation becomes easier to maintain and more usable for a wider range of visitors.
