#10848. DNA robots could deliver drugs and hunt viruses inside your body

Imagine tiny robots made from DNA moving through the bloodstream, delivering drugs exactly where they are needed and targeting threats such as cancer cells or viruses. These microscopic machines could also assemble ultra-precise data storage systems and computing devices at the nanometer scale. Although the possibilities are remarkable, most DNA robots today remain in early experimental stages and are better understood as proof of concept rather than practical tools.

Researchers are exploring how DNA can be engineered into working machines using creative design approaches. These include building rigid DNA joints, incorporating flexible components, and using folding techniques inspired by origami. By applying principles from larger-scale robotics such as rigid, compliant and origami robots, scientists are adapting familiar mechanical concepts to the nanoscale. This allows DNA-based systems to carry out controlled and repeatable tasks despite their extremely small size.

Guiding the motion of DNA robots in a constantly shifting molecular environment is a major challenge. To address this, scientists have developed control systems that help these machines behave in predictable ways. One important method involves DNA strand displacement, a biochemical process that enables precise programming of movement using specific DNA sequences labeled as "fuel" and "structure."

In addition to biochemical control, external physical signals such as electric fields, magnetic fields, and light can direct how these robots move. Together, these approaches provide a toolkit for fine-tuning the behavior of DNA machines with a high degree of accuracy.

The potential uses for DNA robots extend well beyond laboratory experiments. In medicine, they could function as "nano-surgeons," locating diseased cells and delivering targeted treatments with precision. Researchers are also exploring whether these machines could capture viruses like SARS-CoV-2, with future systems potentially operating as fully autonomous drug delivery platforms.

DNA robots may also play a role in advanced manufacturing. Acting as programmable templates, they could position nanoparticles with sub-nanometer accuracy. This capability could lead to breakthroughs in molecular computing and highly efficient optical devices that outperform current technologies.

Despite rapid progress, several obstacles remain. Moving from large-scale systems to molecular machines introduces challenges such as Brownian motion, which makes precise control more difficult. Many current DNA robot designs are still relatively simple and operate in isolation, limiting their usefulness in complex real-world environments.

There are also gaps in foundational knowledge. Researchers still lack detailed databases describing the mechanical properties of DNA structures, and simulation tools for predicting behavior at this scale are not yet fully developed.

To overcome these barriers, scientists emphasize the need for collaboration across disciplines. Proposed solutions include creating standardized DNA "parts libraries," using artificial intelligence to improve design and simulation, and advancing bio-manufacturing methods. Progress in these areas will be essential for scaling DNA robots and integrating them into practical applications in healthcare, manufacturing, and beyond.

"The robots of tomorrow won't just be made of metal and plastic," says the research team. "They will be biological, programmable, and intelligent. They will be the tools that allow us to finally master the molecular world."

#10844. AI breakthrough cuts energy use by 100x while boosting accuracy

Artificial intelligence is consuming enormous amounts of electricity in the United States. According to the International Energy Agency, AI systems and data centers used about 415 terawatt hours of power in 2024. That accounts for more than 10% of the country's total electricity production, and demand is projected to double by 2030.

This rapid growth has raised concerns about sustainability. In response, researchers at a School of Engineering have created a proof-of-concept AI system designed to be far more efficient. Their approach could reduce energy use by up to 100 times while also improving performance on tasks.

A Hybrid Approach Called Neuro-Symbolic AI

The research comes from the laboratory of Matthias Scheutz, Karol Family Applied Technology Professor. His team is developing neuro-symbolic AI, which combines traditional neural networks with symbolic reasoning. This method mirrors how people approach problems by breaking them into steps and categories.

The work will be presented at the International Conference of Robotics and Automation in Vienna in May and will appear in the conference proceedings.

Teaching Robots to See, Understand, and Act

Unlike familiar large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT and Gemini, the team focuses on AI systems used in robotics. These systems are known as visual-language-action (VLA) models. They extend LLM capabilities by incorporating vision and physical movement.

VLA models take in visual data from cameras and instructions from language, then translate that information into real-world actions. For example, they can control a robot's wheels, arms, or fingers to complete a task.

Why Traditional AI Struggles With Simple Tasks

Conventional VLA systems rely heavily on data and trial-and-error learning. If a robot is asked to stack blocks into a tower, it must first analyze the scene, identify each block, and determine how to place them correctly.

This process often leads to mistakes. Shadows may confuse the system about a block's shape, or the robot may place pieces incorrectly, causing the structure to collapse.

These errors are similar to the problems seen in LLMs. Just as robots can misplace blocks, chatbots can generate false or misleading outputs. Examples include fabricating legal cases or producing images with unrealistic details such as extra fingers.

How Symbolic Reasoning Improves Accuracy and Efficiency

Symbolic reasoning offers a different strategy. Instead of relying only on patterns from data, it uses rules and abstract concepts such as shape and balance. This allows the system to plan more effectively and avoid unnecessary trial and error.

"Like an LLM, VLA models act on statistical results from large training sets of similar scenarios, but that can lead to errors," said Scheutz. "A neuro-symbolic VLA can apply rules that limit the amount of trial and error during learning and get to a solution much faster. Not only does it complete the task much faster, but the time spent on training the system is significantly reduced."

The researchers tested their system using the Tower of Hanoi puzzle, a classic problem that requires careful planning.

The neuro-symbolic VLA achieved a 95% success rate, compared with just 34% for standard systems. When given a more complex version of the puzzle that it had not encountered before, the hybrid system still succeeded 78% of the time. Traditional models failed every attempt.

Training time also dropped sharply. The new system learned the task in only 34 minutes, while conventional models required more than a day and a half.

Massive Energy Savings in Training and Use

Energy consumption was reduced dramatically as well. Training the neuro-symbolic model required only 1% of the energy used by a standard VLA system. During operation, it used just 5% of the energy needed by conventional approaches.

Scheutz compared this inefficiency to everyday AI tools. "These systems are just trying to predict the next word or action in a sequence, but that can be imperfect, and they can come up with inaccurate results or hallucinations. Their energy expense is often disproportionate to the task. For example, when you search on Google, the AI summary at the top of the page consumes up to 100 times more energy than the generation of the website listings."

The Growing Strain of AI on Power Infrastructure

As AI adoption accelerates across industries, demand for computing power continues to climb. Companies are building increasingly large data centers, some of which require hundreds of megawatts of electricity. That level of consumption can exceed the needs of entire small cities.

This trend has sparked a race to expand infrastructure, raising concerns about long-term energy limits.

The researchers suggest that current approaches based on LLMs and VLAs may not be sustainable in the long run. While these systems are powerful, they consume large amounts of energy and can still produce unreliable results.

In contrast, neuro-symbolic AI offers a different direction. By combining learning with structured reasoning, it may provide a more efficient and dependable foundation for future AI systems.

Xbox has unveiled one of its most unusual custom consoles yet, placing a fully functioning Xbox Series X inside a life-sized alligator that one lucky fan will get to take home.

The one-of-a-kind creation, called the Xbox Series X-BITE, was revealed on November 3 as part of a sweepstakes inspired by Florida, where Xbox is heading this month.

While the console is housed inside a realistic alligator replica, it remains functional and even comes with a custom controller featuring bite marks.

Measuring more than five feet from snout to tail, the Xbox Series X-BITE features a specially crafted alligator with an Xbox Series X built into its body.

The console is visible through an illuminated Xbox Nexus logo on the creature’s back, while a custom Xbox Wireless Controller sits between its open jaws.

The alligator also features green eyes with pupils inspired by the Xbox logo, along with detailed scales and textures designed to give it a realistic appearance.

Xbox worked with creature animatronics specialists John Nolan Studio to create the custom console. The studio has previously worked on productions including The Witcher, Jurassic World Dominion, and HBO’s upcoming Harry Potter series.

The team used 3D modeling, sculpting, and fabrication techniques to bring the design to life, ensuring the Xbox Series X remained functional inside the finished creation.

Despite its working hardware, Xbox says the custom console is best used as a display piece. The company also confirmed that no real alligators were used or harmed during its creation.

#10840. What “Clear Form” Should Really Do: Managing Draft Data in JavaScript

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

A user fills out a form, requests a preview, and then changes their mind. They click “Clear,” the inputs become empty, and the interface appears ready for someone else.

A moment later, the previous preview returns.

The application cleared the fields, but an asynchronous request still held the old values and updated the screen when it finished. Similar problems occur when drafts remain in browser storage, validation messages retain personal details, or a component’s internal state survives a visual reset.

For developers building onboarding, expense, application, and document workflows, clearing a form is a state-management operation. It deserves the same attention as submission.

This article explains how to define that operation, prevent stale results, and inspect the outcome using practical browser and testing tools.

Start by listing the places where a draft exists. The visible inputs are only one location.

When reviewing a financial-data interface, a useful design exercise is to map which information belongs to the current draft and what should happen when the user starts again. The same exercise applies to expense submissions and customer onboarding; the implementation must be assessed separately from the visible interface.

Name actions according to their actual scope. “Clear this form” should not imply that previously submitted records have been deleted. If a draft has been saved remotely, distinguish clearing the current screen from deleting the saved draft.

For a broader introduction to form structure and validation, SitePoint’s guide to modern HTML forms provides useful background.

Autosave is convenient, but persisting the entire form after every keystroke is an architectural decision, not a harmless UI enhancement.

For a short workflow, keeping the draft in memory may be sufficient. For a longer workflow, decide which fields may be retained, how the user understands that behavior, and when the retained copy is removed.

Browser storage options have different lifetimes. According to MDN’s sessionStorage documentation, session storage is associated with a page session and survives reloads. It should not be treated as equivalent to an ordinary variable that disappears when the page reloads.

Nor does shorter retention make storage a security boundary. The OWASP HTML5 security guidance cautions against storing sensitive information in local storage because JavaScript running in the origin can access it.

This reduces unnecessary copies. It does not provide secure memory erasure or protect a page from every script that can access its data.

The native form.reset() method restores controls to their default values. It does not necessarily make every field empty.

For example, an input rendered with a default value can return to that value after a reset. The method also does not clear a separate preview element, invalidate a network response, or update every framework-managed state variable.

Use a small HTML form with empty defaults for the following example:

The clear control uses type="button" so the application can coordinate the complete operation.

In a React or Vue implementation, apply the same policy to the state that controls the inputs. Clearing the DOM while leaving the component state intact can cause the old values to reappear.

Cancellation helps reduce unnecessary work, but request identity is what protects the interface from a stale result.

Assign each request a generation number. Whenever the draft changes or is cleared, advance that number. A response may update the UI only if its number still matches the current generation.

The following JavaScript works with the HTML above. It assumes a same-origin POST /api/preview endpoint that accepts JSON and returns {"summary":"plain text"}. That endpoint is an integration requirement; it is not implemented here.

Editing a field also invalidates the preview. Otherwise, users could mistake a result based on earlier values for a result based on their current input.

The code writes server-provided text with textContent rather than interpreting it as HTML. It also displays a fixed failure message instead of echoing request values into an error.

AbortController allows the client to abort fetch-related work. Aborting a browser request does not guarantee that server processing stopped or that data already received by the server was deleted.

The generation check enforces the narrower promise: obsolete work must not update this interface. SitePoint’s introduction to the Fetch API explains the request and response mechanics behind the example.

The example intentionally does not save drafts. If your application does, add cleanup to the clear operation rather than assuming that resetting the form handles it.

Remove the application’s specific draft entry. Avoid localStorage.clear() as a general cleanup shortcut, since it also removes unrelated keys for that origin.

Keep the UI honest if storage cleanup fails. Do not announce that every saved copy is gone when the application has only emptied the visible controls.

An object URL should be revoked when it is no longer needed, but revoking it does not delete a file the user already downloaded.

For programmatic changes, call the same invalidation function used by input events. Assigning an input’s value in JavaScript does not automatically trigger the user-input event handler.

You do not need a large dependency stack to verify a clear operation. Each of these tools answers a different question.

Chrome’s local-storage inspection guide explains how to inspect stored entries. Check session storage and IndexedDB too if the application uses them; an empty local-storage table is not proof that no browser persistence exists.

Mock Service Worker is useful for creating reproducible response conditions during development. Use fictional fixtures so debugging sessions do not depend on real personal records.

With Playwright network interception, hold a preview response until the test explicitly releases it. Fill the form, request a preview, clear the draft, and only then release the response. Assert that the input remains empty and the preview never returns.

A controlled release is more reliable than hoping a fixed delay creates the right race. Also test two requests completing in reverse order.

A useful review checks the operation at several points:

Supplement automated accessibility checks with keyboard and screen-reader testing. The Playwright accessibility guide explains that automated checks detect only some accessibility problems.

Verify backend behavior separately. Server validation, authorization, retention, and deletion require their own implementation and tests. A clean browser interface cannot demonstrate those guarantees.

A reliable clear operation has a defined scope. It invalidates pending work, resets the application’s draft state, removes derived output, and handles persistence according to the product’s stated behavior.

The implementation can remain small. What matters is that the team knows where draft data lives and tests what happens when events arrive in an inconvenient order.

When developers make those boundaries explicit, “Clear form” becomes a predictable action rather than a visual reset that leaves the previous workflow running.

#10838. This new chip survives 1300°F (700°C) and could change AI forever

Modern electronics power everything from smartphones to satellites, but they all share a major limitation. Heat. Once temperatures climb above roughly 200 degrees Celsius, most devices begin to break down. For decades, this thermal barrier has been one of the toughest challenges in engineering.

Researchers at the University of Southern California now believe they have found a way past that limit.

In a study published on March 26, 2026 in Science, a team led by Joshua Yang, Arthur B. Freeman Chair Professor at the Ming Hsieh Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering at the USC Viterbi School of Engineering and the USC School of Advanced Computing, unveiled a new type of memory device that continues to operate at 700 degrees Celsius (~1300 degrees Fahrenheit). That temperature exceeds molten lava and goes far beyond anything previously achieved for this class of technology. The device showed no sign of failure. In fact, 700 degrees was simply the maximum their equipment could test.

"You may call it a revolution," Yang said. "It is the best high-temperature memory ever demonstrated."

The new device is known as a memristor, a nanoscale component that can both store data and perform computations. It is constructed like a microscopic layered structure, with two electrodes on either side and a thin ceramic layer in between.

Jian Zhao, the study's first author, built the device using tungsten for the top electrode, hafnium oxide ceramic in the middle, and graphene for the bottom layer. Tungsten has the highest melting point of any element, while graphene, a single-atom-thick sheet of carbon, is known for its exceptional strength and heat resistance.

This combination produced remarkable performance. The device retained data for more than 50 hours at 700 degrees without needing to be refreshed. It also endured over one billion switching cycles at that temperature and operated at just 1.5 volts with speeds measured in tens of nanoseconds.

The discovery was not part of the team's original plan. They were initially attempting to create a different graphene-based device, which did not work as intended. Along the way, they encountered something surprising.

"To be honest, it was by accident, as most discoveries are," Yang said. "If you can predict it, it's usually not surprising, and probably not significant enough."

Further investigation revealed why the device performed so well. In conventional electronics, heat causes metal atoms in the top electrode to slowly migrate through the ceramic layer. Eventually, they reach the bottom electrode, creating a permanent connection that short-circuits the device and leaves it stuck in the on state.

Graphene prevents this failure. Its interaction with tungsten is, as Yang described it, similar to oil and water. Tungsten atoms that approach the graphene surface cannot attach to it. Without a stable point to settle, they drift away instead of forming a conductive bridge. This prevents short circuits and preserves the device's function even under extreme heat.

The researchers confirmed this mechanism using advanced electron microscopy, spectroscopy, and quantum-level simulations. By understanding what happens at the atomic interface, they have turned an unexpected result into a principle that could guide future designs. Other materials with similar surface properties could be identified, which may help scale the technology for industrial production.

Electronics capable of operating above 500 degrees Celsius have long been a goal for space exploration. Venus, for example, has a surface temperature around that level, and every lander sent there has failed in part due to extreme heat. Current silicon-based chips cannot survive such conditions.

"We are now above 700 degrees, and we suspect it will go higher," Yang said.

The potential applications go far beyond space missions. Geothermal energy systems require electronics that can function deep underground, where surrounding rock can glow red-hot. Nuclear and fusion systems also expose equipment to intense heat. Even in everyday settings, durability improves significantly. A device rated for 700 degrees would be extremely robust at the roughly 125-degree temperatures often reached inside automotive electronics.

Why It Matters for Artificial Intelligence

In addition to storing data, the device offers a major advantage for artificial intelligence. Many AI systems rely heavily on matrix multiplication, a mathematical operation used in tasks like image recognition and language processing. Traditional computers perform these calculations step by step, consuming large amounts of energy.

Memristors approach the problem differently. By using Ohm's Law, where voltage times conductance equals current, the device performs calculations directly as electricity flows through it. The result is obtained instantly as the measured current.

"Over 92 percent of the computing in AI systems like ChatGPT is nothing but matrix multiplication," Yang said. "This type of device can perform that in the most efficient way, orders of magnitude faster and at lower energy."

Yang and three co-authors of the study (Qiangfei Xia, Miao Hu, and Ning Ge) have already co-founded a company called TetraMem to commercialize memristor-based AI chips at room temperature. Their lab is already using working chips from TetraMem for machine learning tasks. The high-temperature version described in this research could extend those capabilities to environments where traditional electronics cannot operate, allowing devices such as spacecraft or industrial sensors to process data directly on site.

From Lab Prototype to Real-World Technology

Despite the promising results, Yang emphasizes that practical applications are still some distance away. Memory is only one part of a complete computing system. High-temperature logic circuits will also need to be developed and integrated. In addition, the current devices were built manually at very small scales in a laboratory setting, so manufacturing at scale will take time.

"This is the first step," Yang said. "It's still a long way to go. But logically, you can see: now it makes it possible. The missing component has been made."

From a manufacturing perspective, two of the materials used in the device, tungsten and hafnium oxide, are already widely used in semiconductor production. Graphene is newer but is actively being developed by major companies such as TSMC and Samsung, and it has already been produced at wafer scale in research environments.

The work was conducted through the CONCRETE Center, short for Center of Neuromorphic Computing under Extreme Environments, a multi-university Center of Excellence led by USC and supported by the Air Force Office of Scientific Research and the Air Force Research Laboratory. Key experimental work was carried out in collaboration with Dr. Sabyasachi Ganguli's team at the AFRL Materials Lab in Dayton, Ohio, while theoretical analysis involved USC researchers and collaborators at Kumamoto University in Japan.

For Yang, publication in Science reflects more than a single achievement.

"Space exploration has never been so real, so close, and at such a large scale," he said. "This paper represents a critical leap into a much larger, more exciting frontier."

Materials provided by University of Southern California. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#10837. TikTok dad Marcel Johnson dead aged 32 following stomach cancer

TikTok star Marcel Johnson, who documented his battle with stage 4 stomach cancer while raising five children, has died at the age of 32.

Johnson died on Monday, November 2, following a 15-month battle with cancer. His wife, Taylor Johnson, confirmed the news in an emotional post, revealing that he died at 4:45 PM.

“I lost a whole entire half of me. He fought so hard for so long. He was so tired & exhausted & in so much pain,” she wrote.

Taylor also revealed that her husband’s final words to her and Dedric, spoken earlier that day, were “I’m ready to go.”

“He still fought to hang on all day so we just got a bit more time,” she added.

Taylor said she was struggling to process his death, explaining that she had expected to wake up and find him beside her.

“I love him with my whole entire being and life will absolutely never ever be the same,” she concluded.

Johnson, known online as ‘celnoshell,’ had built a substantial following by documenting his cancer diagnosis, treatments, and family life on TikTok.

The Michigan father of five was diagnosed with stage 4 adenocarcinoma in August 2025 after initially seeking medical attention for stomach pain.

In an interview with WXYZ Detroit, Johnson explained that doctors discovered the cancer within just five days of his initial visit to urgent care.

At the time, he said doctors had told him he would need chemotherapy for the rest of his life.

Alongside his social media presence, Johnson and his wife operated Lil Daddy’s Cheesecakes in Mount Clemens, Michigan.

His diagnosis prompted an outpouring of support from the local community, with neighboring businesses organizing fundraisers and residents donating to help the family cover medical and living expenses.

Johnson continued sharing his journey with hundreds of thousands of followers, including an emotional video in which he explained to his four-year-old son that his cancer treatments were not working.

His death has sparked an outpouring of tributes from viewers who followed his journey over the past year.

Johnson is survived by his wife, Taylor, and their five sons.

Taylor is also requesting that fans avoid using AI to honor Marcel.

“Can we please not AI Marcel and my family?” she said on Facebook. “I know everyone means well, but like that does not look like him or us and I feel it’s a slap in the face.”

#10832. This new chip could slash data center energy waste

As data centers consume more energy to support growing digital demands, engineers at the University of California San Diego have introduced a new chip design that could make powering graphics processing units (GPUs) more efficient. The innovation focuses on a key function in electronics: converting high voltages into the lower levels required by computing hardware. In laboratory testing, a prototype chip successfully performed this type of voltage conversion with high efficiency under conditions similar to those found in modern data centers.

The findings, published in Nature Communications, suggest the potential for smaller and more energy-efficient systems in advanced computing environments.

Rethinking DC-DC Converters for Modern Electronics

At the center of the new design is an improved version of a widely used component known as a DC-DC step-down converter. These converters are found in nearly all electronic devices and serve as a critical link between power sources and sensitive circuits. Their job is to take a high incoming voltage and reduce it to the exact level needed for safe operation.

In data centers, electricity is often distributed at 48 volts, while GPU processors typically require much lower voltages, usually between 1 and 5 volts. Efficiently managing this large voltage drop has become increasingly challenging as computing systems grow more powerful and compact.

Limits of Traditional Power Conversion Technology

Conventional step-down converters often struggle when dealing with large differences between input and output voltage. As that gap increases, efficiency drops and it becomes harder to supply enough current. Most existing designs rely on magnetic components such as inductors. While these components have been refined over many years, they are approaching their practical limits and are becoming harder to improve further.

"We've gotten so good at designing inductive converters that there's not really much room left to improve them to meet future needs," said study senior author Patrick Mercier, professor in the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering at the UC San Diego Jacobs School of Engineering.

Exploring Piezoelectric Resonators as an Alternative

To move beyond these limitations, Mercier and his team, including first author Jae-Young Ko, an electrical and computer engineering Ph.D. student at UC San Diego, investigated a different approach using piezoelectric resonators. These small devices store and transfer energy through mechanical vibrations rather than magnetic fields.

Converters based on piezoelectric components could offer several advantages. They have the potential to be smaller, more energy dense, more efficient, and easier to manufacture at scale. "They have a lot of room to grow and have the potential to deliver better performance than anything that's come before them," Mercier said.

However, earlier versions of piezoelectric converters have had difficulty maintaining efficiency and delivering sufficient power when handling large voltage differences.

Hybrid Design Achieves High Efficiency and Power Output

To overcome these issues, the researchers created a hybrid converter that combines a piezoelectric resonator with small, commercially available capacitors arranged in a carefully designed configuration. This setup enables the system to handle larger voltage conversions more effectively.

The team incorporated this design into a prototype chip and tested its performance. The device successfully converted 48 volts down to 4.8 volts -- a level commonly required in data centers -- with a peak efficiency of 96.2 percent. It also delivered roughly four times more output current than previous piezoelectric-based designs.

This hybrid approach offers several benefits. It creates multiple pathways for energy to move through the system, reduces wasted power, and lessens the strain on the resonator. Together, these improvements enhance both efficiency and power delivery while only slightly increasing the chip's size.

Challenges and Next Steps for Real-World Use

Although the technology shows strong promise, it is still in the early stages of development. The researchers view it as an important step toward overcoming the constraints of current power conversion systems. Future efforts will focus on refining materials, improving circuit designs, and developing better packaging methods.

One challenge is that piezoelectric resonators physically vibrate, which means they cannot be attached to circuit boards using standard soldering techniques. New integration strategies will be needed to incorporate them into electronic systems, Mercier explained.

"Piezoelectric-based converters aren't quite ready to replace existing power converter technologies yet," Mercier added. "But they offer a trajectory for improvement. We need to continue to improve on multiple areas -- materials, circuits and packaging -- to make this technology ready for data center applications."

This project was supported in part by the Power Management Integration Center (PMIC), an Industry-University Cooperative Research Center (IUCRC) funded by the National Science Foundation (award number 2052809).

#10828. Cyberpunk: Edgerunners Season 2 is more than a retread of Netflix's beloved first season - it's a story that truly understands what it means to exist in Night City

Last night, I sat down with a greasy pizza and a few bottles of beer and braced myself for 10 episodes of heartbreak. Cyberpunk: Edgerunners' second season is out, and it follows in the footsteps of Studio Trigger's beloved, and tragic, debut. My expectations were way off.

Not because it wasn't good: Edgerunners Season 2 is fantastic. Packed with a wonderful cast of troubled characters, their story brought to life with gorgeous and often unorthodox animation. The soundtrack, the voice acting... Quality-wise the bar is as high as the first season. What surprised me was the decision to bring something many may find peculiar given Cyberpunk's dire setting and desperate energy. The show is hopeful. Defiant, even.

In the show's opening episode, we are introduced to characters at rock bottom. King, having suffered from cyberpsychosis, has had his augmentations stripped out of his body, and lost his home. D's in the midst of a lonely journey of revenge, while Talia is rubbing elbows with the Maelstrom gang. Roman, a 12-year-old, is broke and struggling to pursue filmmaking in a world that's left the medium behind. In the pursuit of money, he is nearly diced up.

These characters have all the reason in the world to lose themselves to despair, to burn out. Some almost do. However, as the season progresses, they each find a reason to push on, to live in spite of the odds. By the end of the season, while their problems may not have vanished, those who can choose to push on regardless of what life may throw at them. There are more smiles and laughs in the final episode than there are in the first. In the world of Cyberpunk, that's surprising. Defiant.

Violence in Cyberpunk: Edgerunners Season 2 is not treated as some awesome, cathartic spectacle. Through the literal lens of Roman, it's seen as the monstrous act it is. Characters are urged to not go out and kill people - even those who arguably deserve it - consistently throughout the show. In the first season, we saw the brutal reality of killing in David's descent into cyberpsychosis. In this season, characters without that particular affliction are confronted with the futility of the act.

Around halfway through the season, a cowering lady is half-heartedly executed by a side character, and the show lingers on the scene as her head slumps down onto the ground. It's a grisly moment, a siren blaring starkly, broadcasting a very simple message: violence is not the answer.

There is a sentiment that there are no good endings in Night City, and it's a fair belief to have. Magda Zych, senior writer at CD Projekt Red, described the game's story as a 'noir tragedy', and the dystopian world of the tabletop RPG presents a similarly sad motif. Crime is rampant, people are victimised for no reason, people are chewed up and spat out. This was true in Mike Pondsmith's original vision for Night City, it was true in Cyberpunk 2077, and it's true in Cyberpunk: Edgerunners Season 2.

So there's courage in living as best you can in spite of the injustice of the world. If the first season of Cyberpunk: Edgerunners could be aligned, roughly, to 2077's 'The Sun' ending (where V charges into Arasaka in a blaze of glory), Season 2 can be seen as a parallel to 'The Star' ending, where V takes what time they have left and spends it with their friends and loved ones, divorced from the grinding reality of Night City's grinding concrete. Some NPCs react to this decision during the credits with scorn; it is the antithesis of the 'burn bright, die young' Edgerunner philosophy.

I imagine this season may not have met the expectations of many viewers, who are left cold by how different it is from the first season. And yeah, it would have been entirely acceptable to rehash the same sort of story we saw in 2022 again here, and many people - including myself - would have loved it. But to choose not to do that, to steer the narrative into a totally different direction, is smart. You might even say... defiant.

#10827. Best AI Brand Mention Tracking Tools for Enterprises in 2026: 6 Tools Compared

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

At a large company, the hard part of buying an AI brand mention tracking tool is procurement. IT asks about single sign-on, legal asks where the data sits, and the marketing team that wanted the tool waits weeks to log in. A pilot on one brand in one market looks cheap, then the other markets, the other teams and SSO arrive and the quote looks nothing like the trial.

That is why a generic "best tools" list helps enterprise buyers less than it should. All the tools below track how often ChatGPT, Gemini and Google's AI answers name your brand. What separates them at enterprise size is everything around the tracking: how many people can log in, how logins are controlled, whether the data can leave the tool and whether it copes with ten markets instead of one.

This guide compares six tools on those points. Peec AI ranks first because it combines unlimited users, enforceable SSO, source-level analysis and a published price ladder. The other five suit different buying situations.

AI brand mention tracking measures how often, where and how favourably AI engines name your brand when buyers ask category questions. A tool runs a fixed prompt set daily across engines such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Google AI Overviews, Google AI Mode and Microsoft Copilot, then reports mention rate (visibility), position inside the answer, sentiment, share of voice against competitors and the sources each answer cited.

For an enterprise, the answers differ by engine, country and product line, and a single visibility number hides most of that. Similarweb's May 2026 figures put ChatGPT at 53.9% of AI chatbot web visits, Gemini at 27.9% and Claude at 9.2%, against roughly 76% for ChatGPT in June 2025. The question "what does AI say about us?" is now spread over at least three engines.

Access and identity. Ask how many users each plan allows, whether SSO is available and on which plan, and whether you can enforce it. Most tools put SSO on their top tier or a custom plan, so budget for an enterprise contract early.

Markets and brands. Check whether the price grows per country, language or brand. Ten markets multiply a prompt set quickly.

Data access. The data has to reach the reporting leadership already reads: CSV export, an API, a BI connector or an MCP server.

Source analysis. A mention rate shows where you stand. Source data shows why, by listing the pages each engine read. Without it you cannot tell whether you are missing because nobody writes about you or because your own pages are not picked up.

Prompt volume and engines. A hundred to a hundred and fifty prompts per brand and market is a realistic start. Check which engines each plan includes and which sit behind add-ons.

Cost at your real workload. Price the tool for the users, markets and prompts you will have in a year, not for the pilot.

Enterprise teams rarely run on the entry tier, so the tables below price two realistic workloads: about 150 prompts, and about 350 prompts on ChatGPT, Google AI Overviews and Google AI Mode with 15 users, both tracked daily on three engines. Price per prompt is the monthly price divided by the prompts the plan includes. Rankscale and AthenaHQ price by answers or credits instead, so Rankscale's rows use the answer volume the workload needs: 150 prompts on three engines over 30 days is 13,500 answers a month, and 350 prompts is 31,500. Profound does not publish prices and is left out of the tables. Treat every figure as directional: enterprise contracts are custom and billed annually, so published self-serve prices show where a negotiation starts, not what you will pay.

Peec AI has the lowest price per prompt in the first table and the lowest monthly price in the second. Scrunch AI's Core plan costs $2.00 per prompt at 125 prompts and five users, and its larger plans are quote-only. Against Rankscale, the only other tool here with a published enterprise price, Peec AI costs 36% less at 150 prompts ($245 against $385) and 37% less at 350 prompts ($495 against $780). Rankscale does include more engines in its price, which Peec AI reserves for Enterprise. On ChatGPT plus both Google surfaces with 15 people logging in, Peec AI is the cheapest of the tools priced in these tables: $495 against $638 for Otterly.AI once Google AI Mode is added, and $780 for Rankscale. Otterly.AI and Rankscale include more engines in their price.

One thing changes these tables: single sign-on. Peec AI, Profound, AthenaHQ, Scrunch AI and Otterly.AI put SSO on Enterprise, and Rankscale puts it on a custom plan. If IT requires SSO, every tool here becomes a quote, and the published prices only show where the negotiation starts. Annual billing takes 15% to 17% off most of these.

Peec AI is a Berlin-based AI search analytics platform with a New York office. It tracks visibility, position, sentiment and share of voice, breaks every answer into the sources the engine read and turns the gaps it finds into prioritised actions. At enterprise scale its pricing is the main difference: users are unlimited on every plan, and Peec does not charge per country or language, with multi-country tracking from the Advanced plan.

Best for: Enterprise teams that want one tool for every market and every team, and need to know which pages to work on, not only where they stand.

Profound suits purchases that have to clear an information security review before anything else. It lists SOC 2, SSO and SAML on Enterprise, and it raised a $96M Series C at a $1B valuation in February 2026, which settles the vendor-risk question quickly.

Best for: Companies where compliance and vendor risk decide the purchase.

AthenaHQ was built by two former Google Search and DeepMind engineers. Its Enterprise plan has the longest feature list of the quote-based tools: SAML and OIDC single sign-on, audit logs, a 2-hour SLA, a dedicated Slack channel and executive dashboards that feed Tableau, Power BI and Looker. An optimisation agent drafts on-page and off-page actions, which suits large companies that have the analysis but not the hands to act on it.

Best for: Enterprises short on people to act on the data, who want BI dashboards and audit logs.

Scrunch AI publishes one self-serve plan and sells everything else through a quote. Core costs $250 a month and includes 125 prompts, 5,000 responses a month, five user licences and Google single sign-on, which is enough for a pilot with a small team.

Best for: Teams that want a published entry price and five users, with nine engines available on Enterprise.

Rankscale is the only tool here where the enterprise price is on the website. Enterprise is $780 a month for 12,000 credits, up to 48,000 answers, with REST API access and a dedicated partner. Claude, Copilot, ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, both Google surfaces, DeepSeek and Mistral are on every paid plan.

Best for: Teams that need a published enterprise price and the widest engine list.

Otterly.AI has the lowest entry price here, with unlimited team members on every plan and unlimited workspaces from the Standard plan, which helps when several business units want their own view. It is a lighter product than the five above, and SSO sits on its Enterprise plan, which starts from 1,000 prompts.

Best for: Business units that want their own workspace at a low price.

The most common mistake is buying for the pilot. A team runs a trial on one brand and one market, picks the tool with the friendliest entry price and finds out in month four that adding other markets, other teams and SSO moves them onto a quote that looks nothing like the trial.

Before you start a trial, write down three numbers: how many people will need to log in within a year, how many markets you sell in, and whether IT will require SSO. Then ask every vendor to price that.

Enterprise AI brand mention tracking is mostly a question of fit with how a large company buys. Peec AI is the strongest overall choice because users and markets do not drive its price, SSO can be enforced, and its source analysis shows what to fix instead of only how you rank.

Profound is the better route when a compliance review decides everything, AthenaHQ when you want BI dashboards and drafted work, Scrunch AI when you want a published entry price with five users, and Rankscale when you need a published enterprise price.

Whichever you pick, price your real workload, ask about SSO first and remember that the tool measures: what moves the number is being on the pages the engines read. The best AI brand mention tracking tools for enterprises are the ones that show you which pages those are.

What does an enterprise AI brand mention tracking tool cost?

Directionally, between $245 and $780 a month on published plans for 150 to 350 daily prompts: Peec AI Pro at $245 and Advanced at $495, Scrunch AI Core at $250 for 125 prompts, Otterly.AI Premium at $489 and Rankscale at $385 to $780. On Peec AI that is $1.41 to $1.63 per prompt with unlimited users. Once SSO is required, every tool here is a custom quote. The spread is driven by users and markets more than by features.

If more than a handful of people will log in, IT will usually ask for it. Every tool here puts SSO on Enterprise or a custom plan, so plan the budget for that contract instead of the self-serve tier.

How many prompts does an enterprise need?

A hundred to a hundred and fifty per brand and market. Start with the questions your sales team hears, then the comparisons buyers make between you and named competitors. More markets multiply the set. More product pages usually should not.

SEO usually owns the measurement. What breaks is the fix, because much of it means getting mentioned on sites you do not control, which sits with PR or communications. Agree that split before you buy.

#10826. “Giant superatoms” could finally solve quantum computing’s biggest problem

Researchers at Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden have introduced a new theoretical design for quantum systems based on what they call "giant superatoms." This concept offers a fresh way to protect, control, and share quantum information, potentially bringing scientists closer to building large-scale quantum computers.

Quantum computers are expected to transform fields like drug discovery and encryption by solving problems that are far beyond the reach of conventional machines. However, progress has been limited by a major challenge known as decoherence. This occurs when quantum bits, or qubits, lose their information due to interactions with their surroundings. Even small amounts of electromagnetic noise can disrupt the fragile quantum states needed for computation.

"Quantum systems are extraordinarily powerful but also extremely fragile. The key to making them useful is learning how to control their interaction with the surrounding environment," says Lei Du, postdoctoral researcher in applied quantum technology at Chalmers.

Lei Du is the lead author of a study that outlines this new type of quantum system. The design is built around giant superatoms, which combine several important features. These systems reduce decoherence, remain stable, and consist of multiple interconnected "atoms" that function together as a single unit.

Giant superatoms bring together two previously separate ideas in quantum physics: giant atoms and superatoms. While each has been studied on its own, this is the first time they have been merged into a single system. These structures behave like atoms but are not found in nature. Instead, they are engineered by scientists (see fact box below).

The idea of giant atoms was first introduced by researchers at Chalmers over a decade ago and is now widely used in the field. A giant atom is typically designed as a qubit (which is the smallest unit of quantum information). Unlike ordinary atoms, it connects to light or sound waves at multiple, physically separated points. This allows it to interact with its environment in several places at once, helping it preserve quantum information.

"Waves that leave one connection point can travel through the environment and return to affect the atom at another point -- similar to hearing an echo of your own voice before you've finished speaking. This self-interaction leads to highly beneficial quantum effects, reduces decoherence and gives the system a form of memory of past interactions," explains Anton Frisk Kockum, Associate Professor of Applied Quantum Physics at Chalmers and co-author of the study.

Although giant atoms have improved understanding of quantum behavior, they have had limitations when it comes to entanglement. Entanglement allows multiple qubits to share a single quantum state and act as one coordinated system, which is essential for powerful quantum computers.

To overcome this limitation, the research team combined giant atoms with the concept of superatoms. A superatom consists of several natural atoms that share the same quantum state and behave collectively as one larger atom.

This combination is expected to make it easier to create complex quantum states needed for quantum communication, networks, and highly sensitive measurement systems.

"A giant superatom may be envisaged as multiple giant atoms working together as a single entity, exhibiting a non-local interaction between light and matter. This enables quantum information from multiple qubits to be stored and controlled within one unit, without the need for increasingly complex surrounding circuitry," explains Lei Du.

"Giant superatoms open the door to entirely new capabilities, giving us a powerful new toolbox. They allow us to control quantum information and create entanglement in ways that were previously extremely difficult, or even impossible," says Janine Splettstoesser, Professor of Applied Quantum Physics at Chalmers and co-author of the study.

Toward Scalable and Practical Quantum Systems

This work creates new possibilities for building quantum systems that are both scalable and reliable. The researchers plan to move from theory toward actually constructing these systems. Their design could also be integrated with other quantum technologies, serving as a building block for connecting different types of quantum platforms.

"There is currently strong interest in hybrid approaches, in which different quantum systems work together, because each has its own strengths," says Anton Frisk Kockum. "Our research shows that smart design can reduce the need for increasingly complex hardware and giant superatoms are bringing us one step closer to practically applicable quantum technology."

More on: Methods for protecting, controlling and distributing quantum information

The study shows that the way giant superatoms interact with light depends on their internal quantum states. This discovery gives researchers greater control over how quantum information moves through a system. They describe two different ways of connecting these structures to achieve useful outcomes.

In one setup, several giant superatoms are closely linked in a specific arrangement. This allows them to pass quantum states between each other without decoherence, meaning no information is lost.

In another setup, the atoms are spaced farther apart but connected in a carefully tuned way so that waves remain synchronized. This makes it possible to direct quantum signals and distribute entanglement over long distances.

Superatoms and giant atoms are engineered systems that behave like atoms rather than naturally occurring ones.

A superatom is a quantum system made up of multiple natural atoms that share a single quantum state and respond to light as one entity.

A giant atom, on the other hand, connects to light or sound waves at several separate points in space. It is called "giant" because it is larger than the wavelength of the light it interacts with.

Giant atoms have defined energy levels and follow the rules of quantum mechanics, yet they can reach sizes of up to millimeters, making them visible to the naked eye. Through electromagnetic or acoustic waves, they can interact with their surroundings at multiple locations at the same time. One way to picture this is as a single atom linked to a wave at several distant points. This unusual setup allows the atom to be influenced by the waves it produces.

#10825. Worker risks his life using soda bottles to extinguish raging electrical fire

A utility worker in Venezuela has gone viral after using bottles of soda to put out a blazing electrical transformer in a dangerous maneuver that could have ended in disaster.

The incident occurred on November 2 in Valle de la Pascua, Venezuela, where a worker reportedly employed by the state-owned electricity company Corpoelec found himself facing a transformer engulfed in flames.

Rather than reaching for a fire extinguisher, however, the man decided to use something considerably less conventional: two-liter bottles of soda, identified as the Venezuelan brand ‘Glup’.

The employee was elevated in the bucket of a maintenance truck when he began shaking the bottles and launching them toward the burning equipment.

Footage of the incident shows the worker throwing the bottles directly at the transformer before immediately ducking for cover as flames erupt toward his position.

Valle de la Pascua Estado Guárico 🚨 Apaga el transformador con refresco, sucedió en Valle de la Pascua… pic.twitter.com/kAzD0GOn5q

He repeated the process three times, with the fire dying down after his efforts.

But how did it actually work? Carbonated drinks contain carbon dioxide (CO2), which can help suppress flames by displacing oxygen, while the liquid itself may have helped cool the burning equipment.

The extraordinary footage quickly spread across social media, with viewers stunned by the worker’s unconventional firefighting technique.

However, experts have warned that the stunt was incredibly dangerous and could have cost the worker his life.

Speaking to Venezuelan outlet El Pitazo, electrical engineer Jesús Olivares explained that the carbon dioxide in fizzy drinks does not make them a safe substitute for specialized fire extinguishers.

He warned that the liquid could conduct electricity, potentially causing a fatal shock, while the sudden bursts of flames also put the worker at serious risk of burns.

Olivares also questioned the apparent lack of protective equipment, noting that the employee appeared to be working without essential safety gear.

Although the flames appeared to subside, the cause of the fire remains unknown, and there has been no confirmation of whether anyone was injured.

#10822. Phantom Blade Zero review

I wasn't around to witness the golden age of Martial Arts cinema, but there are moments in Phantom Blade Zero that make me feel as though I've tumbled through a crack in time onto the set of a kung fu film. There's one particular encounter that sticks in my mind. Approaching a group of enemies in a shaded valley, I slowly raise my sword, and the first enemy rushes at me. Fool. I perfectly parry the blow, performing a slow-motion somersault to land behind him and plant my sword firmly in his back. The next guy comes running in, and I kick him in the face while simultaneously stabbing the previous enemy in the throat. A third joins the fray - this one on horseback - so I boot him off his horse, and use his steed to trample his helpless friend into the dust. Then, at last, there is silence.

This is Phantom Blade Zero at its absolute peak: cinematic, free-flowing, and full of surprises. Its combat channels the seamless motion and creative choreography of the very best kung fu films, with some frankly astonishing combat animations that seem almost limitless in their ingenuity and variety. It's a game of extraordinary beauty, with jaw-dropping landscapes and hugely ambitious combat encounters. If only - if only! - it could maintain this incredible level of fluidity in all areas of its epic tale.

Our adventure takes place in a fantastical, wuxia-flavoured world called the Wulin: a martial underworld where vicious ne'er-do-wells seem to be running riot, and generally making life miserable for regular people who are just trying to live their lives. Truly, a world miles apart from our own. You play as Soul, a warrior and outcast member of an organisation called The Order. Having played through the entirety of the game, I'm still not entirely sure what The Order stands for in terms of values, but I'm sure they originally meant well. I'm also not really sure what I can tell you about the story - we've been asked not to discuss anything that happens in the prologue - so you're all going to have to use your imaginations here. I can tell you it involves betrayal, a protagonist with limited days to live, a revenge mission, and various malevolent entities from another world. All the standard ingredients you need for a fantasy epic, really.

To warn you in advance, it doesn't take long for Phantom Blade Zero to start dumping an absolutely dizzying number of character names, bloodlines, cults and various feuding sects on you. The way the world lore is delivered - often through reams of text in collectible scrolls dotted around the Wulin - is definitely not one of Phantom Blade Zero's strengths. Most of the game's characters have much to say about nothing, offering various platitudes, truisms and declarations of values that are hard to connect with the underlying story. My advice is to just let everything wash over you, and you'll eventually pick up on the main plot points. While the narrative content leaves much to be desired, the storytelling does include some absolute visual treats - even utilising a traditional Chinese art form to do so. Unfortunately I can't actually praise this in full, because we were also asked not to discuss these elements in our reviews.

Anyway, I think we all know why we're here, and that's because the main draw of Phantom Blade Zero is its combat. The FromSoftware influence is evident in so many aspects of this game, from the series of 'bell' checkpoints scattered throughout the world, to the multi-stage bosses that, yes, can deliver one-shot attacks. Regardless of your weapon loadout, the most important thing you can do in a boss battle is correctly dodge red attacks, and parry blue ones. It's the single most effective way of breaking a boss's guard so that you can enter a punishment phase, and finally get your heavy-hitting moves in. It's kinda like high-octane Sekiro. So if you're not a fan of this dodge/parry combat style, this might not be the game for you.

Perhaps Soulslite would be the better term for Phantom Blade Zero, as there are a lot of clever adjustments here that allow for much speedier combat than other Soulslikes would permit. There isn't a traditional stamina bar, but instead a resource called 'sha-chi', which depletes when you block or parry enemy attacks and when you use heavy attacks. It's a nifty way to allow players to use quick attacks, sprints and dodges without costing stamina. Tied to this is Phantom Blade Zero's two-weapon system, which promotes regular switching between main weapons. If you're running low on sha-chi using one weapon, simply swap to the other and - ta dah! - you have a fresh sha-chi bar to work with (although there is a slight cooldown to prevent total abuse of this mechanic).

This is particularly useful when you want to get some heavy hits in, or if you need to prevent your guard from being broken, which happens when your sha-chi runs low. Another welcome adjustment is that the parry and dodge windows feel really quite generous, which is essential when enemies attacks are coming at you with such speed. If you need to do a last-minute parry, you can cancel nearly any of your moves to do so, which prevents that infuriating problem where you end up locked into an attack juuust as the boss raises their big meat cleaver right above your noggin. The greatest mercy of all is that if you're killed during the second phase of a boss fight, you can just re-enter the boss fight at the start of that second phase. It makes your failures slightly less heartbreaking, and gives you a chance to hop right back into the action with a full set of resources to play with.

Then there are the weapons themselves, which are incredibly flashy and give you access to some genuinely exciting abilities. One sword requires you to tank up on booze, then allows you to send the weapon flying around through the air to attack enemies at range - an enjoyably silly moveset which may not be the most effective build, but which is still fun to play nonetheless. Later you get pole-like swords that can charge through enemies, twin swords that rotate in orbit around you, and a weapon that can summon flowers out of the ground to drain an opponent's sha-chi. There's definitely a process of mastering these weapons and understanding how best to use their abilities in combat - particularly because each has its own unique combinations that are gradually unlocked as you find upgrade materials around the world. Eventually, you find quest items which allow you to 'soul temper' weapons to unlock their most powerful latent abilities, which can suddenly transform an underpowered weapon into something really quite viable (hello again, drunken sword). There's also a class of secondary weapons, known as phantom edges, which are intended for use as additional tools you can draw on in battle to solve problems like high boss guards or unblockable attacks. I constantly experimented with weapons to get a feel for them, and was able to fine-tune my build so that I had a loadout for dealing with large numbers of enemies, and another loadout for breaking boss guards. I got into a real rhythm with the combat, and knew exactly which order in which to pull my moves to maximise my damage.

Against regular enemies found around the Wulin, these weapons feel extraordinary. The combat achieves that perfect kung-fu flow state, and you can bounce around between enemies parrying their blows, lowering their guards, and opening them up for executions. I adore how generous Phantom Blade Zero is with these executions - hit a QTE at the right time, and you can take out two enemies at once. There also seems to be a never-ending supply of these animations: Soul will often use the enemy's own weapons against them, meaning you'll still be finding brand new execution moves 30 hours into the game. It makes the combat constantly surprising, giving variety to the encounters and encouraging you to be aggressive to unlock these deadly finishers. On the regular pathfinder difficulty, the normal enemies feel really well-balanced - you get that sense of flow, but it's absolutely still possible to mess things up if you go charging in without the right loadout, or without priorisiting ranged enemies first.

Against boss enemies, however, these once-powerful weapons are suddenly defanged. During my playthrough, a very high proportion of the bosses felt spongy - especially on pathfinder mode, but even if you lowered the difficulty to wayfarer, which is supposed to be the fun 'rampage through the game' difficulty setting. The weapons which felt so effective against other enemies suddenly became toothpicks against these bosses, even during their punishment phases. Successfully parrying or dodging was rewarded with a very minor dink to a boss's sha-chi, instantly giving you that sinking feeling that you're in for a very long, repetitive fight.

In a Soulslike game, low damage is normally a hint to start experimenting with your build or to try different weapons to see if you can find the 'key' to a boss fight, but Phantom Blade Zero is not very good at communicating exactly what these might be. As an example, one early obligatory boss fight sees you fight an enemy with a spiked shield, and attacking said enemy causes you to start bleeding. It's obvious that you need to break the shield, and that you need to use one of the game's secondary weapons to do so - but when you use the axe phantom edge, very little happens, and that lack of reactivity caused me to go back walking through the world thinking I'd missed something. Turns out I was on the right track, and just needed to keep spamming the move or do a 'charged' version of it (which the game doesn't exactly encourage, as the wind-ups for these charged phantom edge moves are so long that they're normally not viable in the middle of a fast-paced battle). In another case, a phantom edge which shoots water - and is specifically described as being effective against fire types - did absolutely nothing against a fire type enemy. I often didn't feel rewarded for testing these different phantom edges, and the sponginess of the bosses, particularly in the early to mid game when your build options are limited, made a lot of these battles feel artificially lengthy.

This is one of my main gripes with the game, but this is also where things get… interesting. Two days before the review embargo was due to lift, developer S-Game released a 67GB update targeting performance and bugs, along with boss, enemy, ability and weapon stats. "These changes aim to make the difficulty curve feel smoother, both in boss fights and as you progress through each area," we were told. Obviously, this did not give me time to replay the entire game to see if the changes made a difference to the overall experience. I did return to some old save files and found that the sponginess remained present in several boss fights - especially those early obligatory ones - so it appears to still be an issue. It's possible that the launch build will allow player parries, dodges and weapons to feel a little more effective against bosses - but alas, I can only write about the version of the game I've played.

Despite the variety of animations and move sets used by the bosses, a lot of these battles also seem to fall into a fairly strict defend/attack pattern where you don't have much opportunity to disrupt enemy movesets. But that's not to say all boss battles feel exactly the same. Those with multiple smaller enemies allow you to feel like you're doing more damage, while some of the most memorable battles break out of the standard pattern to bring in something totally different. One boss fires missiles horizontally like a bullet hell, while another sees you dance on top of poles while exchanging cannon fire with your enemy. The latter was absolutely fantastic: visually stunning, unexpected, and a moment of pure unadulterated fun.

Of course, an essential part of any Soulslike/lite is noodling around the world to find upgrades and blow off steam between boss fights, and praise should go to the exploration aspect of Phantom Blade Zero. The world map is formed of traditional hand-painted ink wash paintings, with mists that part to reveal new areas with each bell you discover. These beautiful maps only hint at what you'll encounter in each area: you have to find your way through by observing the landscape and spotting hidden pathways on foot. There are plenty of 'aha' moments where you finally find the way up to a distant chest on a cliff that you'd spotted a while back. The Metroidvania elements of the game similarly build anticipation for being able to return to an area, with the phantom edge weapons you unlock through the main story later giving you access to previously-locked areas. S-Game does occasionally overcook this by placing too many closed doors next to each other: on entering the game's main city, I encountered a cluster of seven locked areas within the first few streets, which was a bit dispiriting. No room at the inn for poor old Soul, it seems. My advice is to really take your time in your initial exploration of an area, and not rush to the next region until you're fairly certain you've explored as much as you can at that stage. It's hard to see from the world map what you might have missed - and because enemies don't respawn, retraversing through these levels later on can feel weirdly empty.

Phantom Blade Zero has some extraordinary highs, but a gradual build-up of niggles eventually starts to weigh on you during a playthrough. It's a death by a thousand cuts, of things that really should have been caught during play testing. There's an essential key that's easy to miss because it glows orange and is placed next to a fire of the same colour. It's easy to get caught on geometry, and you end up doing much of your fighting against walls when you push your enemies there with long-combination attack patterns. On several occasions bosses hopped outside their arenas to attack me from behind invisible walls - a sort of reverse cheese that I really didn't appreciate. Certain sidequest missions misdirected me on the map, leaving me going around in circles when it turns out an entirely unrelated quest needed to be completed first. I experienced some severe frame rate dips in certain areas of the game, too - not ideal for a fast-paced action game. These nuisances do stack up, and although S-Game said it has addressed the escaping bosses, performance issues and the quest guidance fails in its latest patch, it's hard to say conclusively whether all of these issues have been fully resolved. The frame rates do seem to be better since the update, but that annoying side quest loop is still in place.

On/off setting for motion blur and camera shake. Adjustable brightness options, two font size options. Independent sliders for music, effects and dialogue. Four difficulty settings. Control scheme screen easily available, full key and button remapping. Can invert Y/X axis. Adjustable controller vibration and sensitivity settings.

All of which leaves us with quite a tricky picture. This game is exceptional in so many areas - the animations, the beautiful environments - and when the combat works, the sense of flow is incredible. Street fights with multiple opponents feel so cinematic and so satisfying, allowing you to be truly creative and expressive with your fighting style. Then you walk into a boss battle and feel all that power fade, like you're waiting your turn to get hits in with a wooden sword. This slows the pace of the early to mid game in particular, and I wish S-Game had been prepared to speed us through to the real meat of its gameplay a little faster. Combined with the other smaller issues and niggles - plus the pretty unremarkable narrative and lore dumps - it just takes the shine off what is otherwise a very impressive action title. Who knows, maybe another patch or two will even things out. Because there are some incredibly fun weapons to play with here… if only they had been sharpened.

A copy of Phantom Blade Zero was provided for this review by S-Game.

#10821. WWE star Danhausen hits back after fans think his facepaint trademark targets Magic: The Gathering

WWE superstar Danhausen has responded to backlash after an old interview about his trademarked facepaint resurfaced online, with some fans believing he was preparing to take legal action against Magic: The Gathering.

Danhausen, whose real name is Donovan Danhausen, is known for his black-and-white facepaint, comedic curses, jars of teeth, and “Very Nice, Very Evil” persona. He joined WWE earlier this year after previously wrestling for AEW and Ring of Honor.

The resurfaced clip came from a 2025 appearance on Insight with Chris Van Vliet. During the interview, Danhausen explained that he had already been wearing his signature makeup when he saw a Magic: The Gathering card with a strikingly similar design. The card was identified in the repost as Juri, Master of the Revue.

The clip prompted some fans to accuse Danhausen of claiming that Wizards of the Coast copied his character. He pushed back against that interpretation on X.

“If you’re mad about this, you’re stupid,” Danhausen wrote. “This isn’t so Danhausen can Willy nilly try to sue people. It’s literally so no one can yell at Danhausen.”

He later replied to another fan, writing, “Bingo. Danhausen loves Magic.”

Danhausen’s facepaint trademark predates his WWE career. The USPTO filing was submitted under his real name in 2020 and describes the mark as a stylized face used across merchandise and wrestling entertainment.

The clarification arrived during a major week for Danhausen, who hosted a WWE YouTube special, appeared in a Danhausen-themed SmackDown episode, and hosted NXT Halloween Havoc.

#10819. This simple change stops robot swarms from getting stuck

Imagine a swarm of robots rushing to complete an urgent job, such as cleaning up an oil spill or assembling complex machinery. At first, adding more robots speeds things up. But after a certain point, the space becomes crowded, robots start interfering with one another, and overall progress slows.

This raises a simple but important question: in a limited area, how many robots can you deploy before efficiency starts to drop? Researchers at Harvard believe they have found a clear answer.

A new study from the lab of L. Mahadevan, the Lola England de Valpine Professor of Applied Mathematics, Organismic and Evolutionary Biology, and Physics, shows that adding a controlled amount of randomness to how robots move can reduce congestion and improve performance in crowded environments.

The work combines mathematical modeling, computer simulations, and real-world experiments. It demonstrates how basic local movement rules can lead to organized, efficient outcomes on a larger scale. The findings could influence how robotic fleets are designed and may even apply to human crowd management and traffic flow. The research was published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences and led by applied mathematics Ph.D. student Lucy Liu, with guidance from SEAS Senior Research Fellow Justin Werfel.

Why Randomness Helps Predict Complex Behavior

Studying dense crowds is difficult because individuals can take countless possible paths and interact in unpredictable ways, Liu explained. To simplify the problem, the researchers treated each robot as a basic unit with a small, adjustable amount of variation in its movement.

"This might be counterintuitive, because how could randomness make things easier to work with?" said Liu. "But in this case, when you have a lot of randomness, it becomes possible to take averages -- average distances, average times, average behaviors. This makes it a lot easier to make predictions."

To explore this idea, the team created computer simulations of robot groups, referred to as agents. Each agent started at a random location and was assigned a random destination. Once it reached its target, it immediately received a new one, mimicking continuous task assignment in real-world systems.

Each agent moved toward its goal with a tunable amount of variation, described as "noise." With no noise, agents moved in straight lines. With high noise, their paths became erratic and inefficient. However, this wandering also helped them navigate around one another.

The simulations revealed a clear pattern. When agents moved in perfectly straight paths, they quickly formed dense clusters and traffic jams that halted progress. When movement became too random, congestion disappeared but efficiency dropped due to excessive wandering.

Between these extremes, the researchers identified a sweet spot. In this range, agents occasionally bumped into one another and formed short-lived clusters, but still managed to slip past and keep moving. This balance allowed the system to maintain a steady flow.

Using these insights, the team developed formulas to estimate "goal attainment rate," or how many destinations are reached over time. These equations made it possible to determine the ideal combination of crowd density and movement randomness to maximize performance.

To confirm their findings, Liu collaborated with physicist Federico Toschi at Eindhoven University of Technology in the Netherlands. Together, they set up experiments with small wheeled robots in a lab equipped with an overhead camera.

Each robot carried a QR code so its position could be tracked and updated with new destinations. Although the physical robots moved more slowly and less precisely than the simulated agents, they displayed the same overall patterns.

The experiments supported a key idea: highly complex coordination does not require advanced intelligence or centralized control. Instead, simple local rules can produce effective group behavior, at least within certain density limits.

"Understanding how active matter, whether it is a swarm of ants, a herd of animals, or a group of robots, become functional and execute tasks in crowded environments using the principles of self-organization, is relevant to many questions in behavioral ecology," Mahadevan said. "Our study suggests strategies that might well be much broader than the instantiation we have focused on."

Liu noted that she has long been interested in designing safer and more efficient crowded spaces. This research points toward a future where the movement of large groups, whether robots, vehicles, or people, could be predicted and optimized using mathematical tools.

The results suggest that introducing controlled variability into movement patterns may improve flow in many real-world systems, from factory floors to city streets.

Funding for the research came from the National Science Foundation Graduate Research Fellowship Program under Grant No. DGE 2140743, along with grants from the Simons Foundation and the Henri Seydoux Fund.

Materials provided by Harvard John A. Paulson School of Engineering and Applied Sciences. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
